children.translated_text: Now, the word ‘atha’ has the sense of beginning an authorized topic.
One should understand that the discipline of yoga is the authoritative treatise now undertaken.

children.text: yogaḥ samādhiḥ sa ca sārvabhaumaścittasya dharmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Yoga is samādhi; and it is a property of the mind that applies on every level.

children.text: kṣiptaṃ mūḍhaṃ vikṣiptaṃ ekāgraṃ niruddham iti cittabhūmayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The stages of the mind are called restless, dull, distracted, one-pointed, and restrained.

children.text: tatra vikṣipte cetasi vikṣepopasarjanībhūtaḥ samādhir na yogapakṣe vartate ||
children.translated_text: Among these, when the mind is distracted, a samādhi that has distraction as its subsidiary does not belong to the side of yoga.

children.text: yas tv ekāgre cetasi sadbhūtam arthaṃ pradyotayati kṣiṇoti ca kleśān karmabandhanāni ślathayati nirodham abhimukhaṃ karoti sa samprajñāto yoga ity ākhyāyate ||
children.translated_text: But that which, in a one-pointed mind, illuminates a real object, weakens the afflictions, loosens the bonds of karma, and turns the mind toward restraint, is called samprajñāta yoga.

children.text: sa ca vitarkānugato vicārānugata ānandānugato 'smitānugata iti upariṣṭāt pravedayiṣyāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And that, as we shall explain later, is accompanied by vitarka, accompanied by vicāra, accompanied by bliss, and accompanied by I-am-ness.
But when all mental activities are restrained, there is asaṃprajñāta samādhi.
In order to state its defining mark, this sūtra has begun.
Because the word ‘all’ is used, samprajñāta too is called yoga.
For the mind, by its nature of illumination, activity, and stability, consists of the three guṇas.

children.text: prakhyārūpaṃ hi cittasattvam rajastamobhyāṃ saṃsṛṣṭam aiśvaryaviṣayapriyaṃ bhavati
children.translated_text: The sattva of the mind, whose form is illumination, when mixed with rajas and tamas, becomes fond of power and its objects.

children.text: tad eva tamasā anuviddham adharmājñānāvairāgyānaiśvaryopagaṃ bhavati
children.translated_text: That very same mind, pierced by tamas, becomes joined with adharma, ignorance, non-dispassion, and lack of power.

children.text: tad eva prakṣīṇamohāvaraṇaṃ sarvataḥ pradyotamānam anuviddhaṃ rajomātrayā dharmajñānavairāgyaiśvaryopagaṃ bhavati
children.translated_text: That very same mind, when the covering of delusion has been diminished and it shines everywhere, pierced only by rajas, becomes joined with dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and power.

children.text: tad eva rajoleśamalāpetaṃ svarūpapratiṣṭhaṃ sattvapuruṣānyatākhyātimātraṃ dharmameghadhyānopagaṃ bhavati
children.translated_text: That very same mind, free from the impurity of even a trace of rajas, established in its own nature, consisting solely in the discernment of the difference between sattva and puruṣa, becomes joined with the dharma-cloud meditation.

children.text: tat paraṃ prasaṃkhyānam ity ācakṣate dhyāyinaḥ
children.translated_text: Meditators call that supreme prasaṃkhyāna, discriminative insight.

children.text: citiśaktir apariṇāminī apratisaṃkramā darśitaviṣayā śuddhā cānantā ca
children.translated_text: The power of consciousness is unchanging, does not pass over into another, has objects presented to it, and is pure and infinite.

children.text: sattvaguṇātmikā ceyam ato viparītā vivekakhyātir iti
children.translated_text: But this mind is of the nature of the sattva-guṇa and is therefore the opposite; this is discriminative knowledge.

children.text: atas tasyāṃ viraktaṃ cittaṃ tām api khyātiṃ niruṇaddhi tadavasthaṃ cittaṃ saṃskāropagaṃ bhavati sa nirbījaḥ samādhiḥ na tatra kiṃcit samprajñāyata iti asaṃprajñātaḥ
children.translated_text: Therefore, when the mind becomes dispassionate toward that knowledge and restrains even that discernment, the mind in that state is accompanied only by saṃskāras. That is seedless samādhi; since nothing is distinctly cognized there, it is asaṃprajñāta.
Thus that twofold yoga is the restraint of the activities of the mind.

children.text: tadavasthe cetasi svaviṣayābhāvāt buddhibodhātmā puruṣaḥ kiṃsvabhāvaḥ iti ||
children.translated_text: When the mind is in that state, because its own objects are absent, what is the nature of puruṣa, whose essence is the awareness of buddhi?

children.text: svarūpapratiṣṭhā tadānīṃ citiśaktir yathā kaivalye vyutthānacitte tu sati tathāpi bhavantī na tathā ||
children.translated_text: At that time the power of consciousness is established in its own nature, as in kaivalya; but when there is an arisen mind it exists, though not in that same way.
How then?
Because objects are presented to it.
In the state of arising, puruṣa has activities not different from the activities of the mind.
And so there is the sūtra:

children.text: ekam eva darśanaṃ khyātir eva darśanam iti
children.translated_text: ‘Seeing is one alone; knowledge itself is seeing.’

children.text: cittam ayaskāntamaṇikalpaṃ saṃnidhimātropakāri dṛśyatvena svaṃ bhavati puruṣasya svāminaḥ
children.translated_text: The mind, like a lodestone, helps merely by proximity; as something seen, it becomes the property of puruṣa, its master.
Therefore the beginningless relation of puruṣa is the cause in the cognition of the activities of the mind.

children.text: tāḥ punar niroddhavyā bahutve sati cittasya ||
children.translated_text: Those activities, moreover, must be restrained, since the mind has multiplicity.
Those that arise from the afflictions, and serve as the field for the accumulation of karmic deposits, are afflicted.
Those whose object is discriminative knowledge and which oppose the operation of the guṇas are unafflicted.
Even when fallen into the stream of the afflicted, the unafflicted remain unafflicted.

children.text: kliṣṭacchidreṣv apy akliṣṭā bhavanti akliṣṭacchidreṣu kliṣṭā iti
children.translated_text: And in gaps among the afflicted there are unafflicted activities; in gaps among the unafflicted there are afflicted ones.

children.text: tathājātīyakāḥ saṃskārā vṛttibhir eva kriyante saṃskāraiśca vṛttaya iti
children.translated_text: Saṃskāras of the same kind are produced by the activities themselves, and activities are produced by saṃskāras.
Thus the wheel of activities and saṃskāras turns without ceasing.

children.text: tad evaṃbhūtaṃ cittam avasitādhikāram ātmakalpena vyavatiṣṭhate pralayaṃ vā gacchatīti ||
children.translated_text: Such a mind, when its purpose has been completed, stands apart as if self-like, or else goes to dissolution.
Those activities, afflicted and unafflicted, are of five kinds.

children.text: indriyapraṇālikayā cittasya bāhyavastūparāgāt tadviṣayā sāmānyaviśeṣātmano 'rthasya viśeṣāvadhāraṇapradhānā vṛttiḥ pratyakṣaṃ pramāṇam ||
children.translated_text: Because the mind is colored by external things through the channel of the senses, the activity concerning that object, whose nature is general and particular and whose chief function is determination of the particular, is direct perception, a pramāṇa.
Its result is the cognition by puruṣa of a mental activity not different from that object.
We shall later establish that puruṣa is the one who experiences the buddhi.

children.text: anumeyasya tulyajātīyeṣv anuvṛtto bhinnajātīyebhyo vyāvṛttaḥ saṃbandho yaḥ tadviṣayā sāmānyāvadhāraṇapradhānā vṛttiḥ anumānam ||
children.translated_text: The relation belonging to what is to be inferred, continuing among things of the same class and excluded from things of a different class, is the object of an activity whose chief function is determination of the general; that is inference.
For example, because the moon and stars reach another region, they possess motion, like <s>Caitra</s>.
And the <s>Vindhya</s>, because it does not reach another region, is motionless.

children.text: āptena dṛṣṭo 'numito vārthaḥ paratra svabodhasaṃkrāntaye śabdenopadiśyate śabdāt tadarthaviṣayā vṛttiḥ śrotur āgamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: An object seen or inferred by a trustworthy person is taught elsewhere by words so that his own cognition may pass into another; from the word, the hearer’s activity concerning that object is verbal testimony.

children.text: yasyāśraddheyārtho vaktā na dṛṣṭānumitārthaḥ sa āgamaḥ plavate mūlavaktari tu dṛṣṭānumitārthe nirviplavaḥ syāt ||
children.translated_text: If the speaker’s meaning is untrustworthy and he has not seen or inferred the object, that testimony wavers; but when the original speaker has seen or inferred the object, it is unwavering.
Why is that not a pramāṇa?
Because it is contradicted by a pramāṇa.
For a pramāṇa has a real object as its sphere.
There, contradiction of a non-pramāṇa by a pramāṇa is observed.
For example:
The perception of two moons is contradicted by the perception of one moon, whose object is real.

children.text: seyaṃ pañcaparvā bhavaty avidyā avidyāsmitārāgadveṣābhiniveśāḥ kleśā iti
children.translated_text: This avidyā has five divisions: ignorance, I-am-ness, attachment, aversion, and clinging to life are the afflictions.

children.text: eta eva svasaṃjñābhiḥ tamo moho mahāmohas tāmisro 'ndhatāmisra iti
children.translated_text: These same are, under their own names, darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, and blind gloom.
These will be explained in connection with the impurities of the mind.

children.text: sa na pramāṇopārohī na viparyayopārohī ca
children.translated_text: It does not rise onto pramāṇa, nor does it rise onto error.
Even when there is no real object, worldly usage is seen to be founded on the power of verbal cognition.
For example:
'Consciousness is the own-nature of the <s>puruṣa</s>.'

children.text: yadā citir eva puruṣas tadā kim atra kena vyapadiśyate
children.translated_text: When consciousness itself is the <s>puruṣa</s>, what, in this case, is designated by what?
And in designation there is an operation of usage.
As in:
'The cow of <s>Caitra</s>.'
So too:

children.text: pratiṣiddhavastudharmā niṣkriyaḥ puruṣaḥ tiṣṭhati bāṇaḥ sthāsyati sthita iti
children.translated_text: The <s>puruṣa</s>, whose object-properties are denied and who is inactive, is spoken of as 'standing,' 'the arrow will stand,' and 'stood.'
When motion has ceased, only the bare verbal-root meaning is understood.

children.text: tathā anutpattidharmā puruṣa iti utpattidharmasyābhāvamātram avagamyate na puruṣānvayī dharmaḥ
children.translated_text: Likewise, in the statement 'the <s>puruṣa</s> has the property of non-origination,' only the mere absence of the property of origination is understood, not a property inhering in the <s>puruṣa</s>.

children.text: tasmāt vikalpitaḥ sa dharmaḥ tena cāsti vyavahāra iti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore that property is imagined, and by means of it there is ordinary usage.
And that sleep is a particular cognition, because on awakening there is reflective recollection of it.
How so?

children.text: sukham aham asvāpsam prasannaṃ me manaḥ prajñāṃ me viśāradīkaroti
children.translated_text: 'I slept happily; my mind is clear and makes my understanding lucid.'

children.text: duḥkham aham asvāpsam styānaṃ me mano bhramaty anavasthitam
children.translated_text: 'I slept unhappily; my mind is dull, wandering, and unsteady.'

children.text: gāḍhaṃ mūḍho 'ham asvāpsam gurūṇi me gātrāṇi klāntaṃ me cittam ālasaṃ muṣiṭam iva tiṣṭhatīti
children.translated_text: 'I slept deeply, as if stupefied; my limbs are heavy, my mind is weary, and it remains idle, as if stolen away.'

children.text: sa khalv ayaṃ pratyavamarśo na syād asati pratyayānubhave
children.translated_text: This reflective recollection would not occur if there had been no experience of a cognition.
And memories based on that experience and having it as their object would not occur.
Therefore sleep is a particular cognition.

children.text: sā ca samādhāv itarapratyayavan niroddhavyā iti ||
children.translated_text: And in samādhi it too, like other cognitions, is to be restrained.

children.text: kiṃ pratyayasya cittaṃ smarati āhosvid viṣayasyeti ||
children.translated_text: Does the mind remember the cognition, or rather the object?

children.text: grāhyoparaktaḥ pratyayo grāhyagrahaṇobhayākāranirbhāsas tajjātīyakaṃ saṃskāram ārabhate ||
children.translated_text: A cognition, colored by the grasped object and appearing in the forms of the grasped, the grasping, and both, initiates an impression of the same kind.

children.text: sa saṃskāraḥ svavyañjakāñjanas tadākārām eva grāhyagrahaṇobhayātmikāṃ smṛtiṃ janayati ||
children.translated_text: That impression, when an activating collyrium is applied to it, produces memory having precisely that form, consisting of both the grasped and the grasping.
In that case, intellect is preceded by the form of grasping.
Memory is preceded by the form of the grasped object.

children.text: sā ca dvayī bhāvitasmartavyā ca abhāvitasmartavyā ca ||
children.translated_text: And that memory is twofold: with what is to be remembered already presented, and with what is to be remembered not already presented.
In dream, what is to be remembered has been presented.
But in the waking state, what is to be remembered has not been presented.
All these memories arise from experiences of valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory.
And all these fluctuations have the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Pleasure, pain, and delusion are to be explained among the afflictions.

children.text: sukhānuśayī rāgaḥ duḥkhānuśayī dveṣo mohaḥ punar avidyeti ||
children.translated_text: Attachment rests upon pleasure; aversion rests upon pain; and delusion, again, is ignorance.
All these fluctuations are to be restrained.

children.text: āsāṃ nirodhe samprajñāto vā samādhir bhavaty asaṃprajñāto veti ||
children.translated_text: When they are restrained, samādhi is either samprajñāta, with cognitive content, or asaṃprajñāta, without such cognitive content.
Now, what is the means for restraining them?

children.text: cittanadī nāma ubhayatovāhinī vahati kalyāṇāya vahati pāpāya ca
children.translated_text: The so-called river of the mind flows in two directions: it flows toward the good and also toward evil.

children.text: yā tu kaivalyaprāgbhārā vivekaviṣayanimnā sā kalyāṇavahā
children.translated_text: That which slopes toward discernment, bearing onward toward kaivalya, is the stream flowing toward the good.
That which slopes toward nondiscernment, bearing onward toward saṃsāra, is the stream flowing toward evil.

children.text: tatra vairāgyeṇa viṣayasrotaḥ khilīkriyate vivekadarśanābhyāsena vivekasrota udghāṭyata ity ubhayādhīnaścittavṛttinirodhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, by dispassion the stream toward objects is made barren, and by the practice of discriminative vision the stream of discernment is opened; thus the restraint of mental fluctuations depends on both.
The steadiness of a mind without fluctuations is a tranquil flow.
The effort directed toward that is vigor, energy.
Practice is the undertaking of the means to accomplish that, from the desire to bring it fully about.

children.text: dīrghakālāsevito nirantarāsevitaḥ satkārāsevitaḥ tapasā brahmacaryeṇa vidyayā śraddhayā ca sampāditaḥ satkāravān dṛḍhabhūmir bhavati vyutthānasaṃskāreṇa drāg ity evānabhibhūtaviṣaya ity arthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When cultivated for a long time, cultivated without interruption, cultivated with reverence, and brought to completion through austerity, celibacy, knowledge, and faith, it becomes reverent and firmly grounded; that is, it is not quickly overwhelmed by the impression of emergence from concentration.

children.text: striyo 'nnapānam aiśvaryam iti dṛṣṭaviṣaye vitṛṣṇasya svargavaidehyaprakṛtilayatvaprāptāv ānuśravikaviṣaye vitṛṣṇasya divyādivyaviṣayasaṃprayoge 'pi cittasya viṣayadoṣadarśinaḥ prasaṃkhyānabalād anābhogātmikā heyopādeyaśūnyā vaśīkārasaṃjñā vairāgyam ||
children.translated_text: Dispassion called mastery is the non-thirst of one who has become free of craving for seen objects such as women, food and drink, and lordly power, and for scripturally heard objects such as attainment of heaven, bodilessness, or dissolution into primordial nature; even when in contact with divine and non-divine objects, the mind, seeing the defects in objects, through the power of discriminative knowledge, is without engagement and empty of what is to be rejected or accepted.

children.text: dṛṣṭānuśravikaviṣayadoṣadarśī viraktaḥ puruṣadarśanābhyāsāt tacchuddhipravivekāpyāyitabuddhir guṇebhyo vyaktāvyaktadharmakebhyo virakta iti
children.translated_text: One who sees the defects in seen and scripturally heard objects is dispassionate; through the practice of seeing the <s>puruṣa</s>, his intellect is nourished by discrimination of that purity, and he is dispassionate toward the guṇas, which possess manifest and unmanifest properties.
That dispassion is twofold.

children.text: tatra yad uttaraṃ taj jñānaprasādamātram yasyodaye yogī pratyuditakhyātir evaṃ manyate
children.translated_text: Of these, the higher one is merely the clarity of knowledge; when it arises, the yogin, whose insight has arisen, thinks as follows:

children.text: prāptaṃ prāpaṇīyaṃ kṣīṇāḥ kṣetavyāḥ kleśāḥ chinnaḥ śliṣṭaparvā bhavasaṃkramaḥ yasyāvicchedāj janitvā mriyate mṛtvā ca jāyata iti
children.translated_text: 'What was to be attained has been attained; the afflictions that were to be destroyed have been exhausted; the connected joints of the passage through becoming have been cut, because of whose uninterrupted continuity one is born and dies, and having died is born again.'
The very highest limit of knowledge is dispassion.
Indeed kaivalya is the immediate consequence of this alone.
Vitarka is the coarse taking-up of the mind toward its support.
Vicāra is subtle.
Ānanda is delight.
Asmitā is unitary awareness.
Among these, the first samādhi, accompanied by the fourfold set, is savitarka.
The second, lacking vitarka, is savicāra.
The third, lacking vicāra, is sānanda.
The fourth, lacking that, is mere asmitā.
All these are samādhis with an object-support.
Now, what is the means of asaṃprajñāta samādhi, and what is its nature?
When all fluctuations have set, the restraint of the mind in which only impressions remain is asaṃprajñāta samādhi.
Its means is supreme dispassion.

children.text: sālambano hy abhyāsas tatsādhanāya na kalpata iti virāmapratyayo nirvastuka ālambanīkriyate
children.translated_text: For practice with a support is not fit to serve as the means to that; therefore a cessation-cognition, devoid of an object, is made the support.
And it is empty of an object.

children.text: tadabhyāsapūrvaṃ cittaṃ nirālambanam abhāvaprāptam iva bhavatīty eṣa nirbījaḥ samādhir asaṃprajñātaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The mind, preceded by practice of that, becomes supportless, as though it had reached non-being. This is seedless samādhi, asaṃprajñāta.
Now this is of two kinds:
dependent on means and dependent on becoming.
Among these, what is dependent on means belongs to yogins.
What is dependent on becoming belongs to the bodiless gods.

children.text: te hi svasaṃskāramātropayogena cittena kaivalyapadam ivānubhavantaḥ svasaṃskāravipākaṃ tathājātīyakam ativāhayanti
children.translated_text: For they, with minds functioning only through their own saṃskāras, experience something like the state of kaivalya and pass through the ripening of their own saṃskāras, which is of that same kind.

children.text: tathā prakṛtilayāḥ sādhikāre cetasi prakṛtilīne kaivalyapadam ivānubhavanti yāvan na punar āvartate 'dhikāravaśāc cittam iti ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, those dissolved in prakṛti, while the mind whose function still remains is dissolved in prakṛti, experience something like the state of kaivalya until, through the force of that function, the mind returns again.
What is dependent on means belongs to yogins.
Faith is the clarity and serenity of the mind.

children.text: sā hi jananīva kalyāṇī yoginaṃ pāti
children.translated_text: For she, beneficent like a mother, protects the yogin.

children.text: tasya hi śraddadhānasya vivekārthino vīryam upajāyate
children.translated_text: In one who has faith and seeks discriminative discernment, energy arises.
When energy has arisen, mindfulness becomes present.
When mindfulness is present, the mind, undisturbed, becomes concentrated.

children.text: samāhitacittasya prajñāviveka upāvartate yena yathārthaṃ vastu jānāti
children.translated_text: For one whose mind is concentrated, discriminative insight comes near, by which one knows the thing as it really is.

children.text: tadabhyāsāt tadviṣayāc ca vairāgyād asaṃprajñātaḥ samādhir bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Through practice of that, and through dispassion toward its object, asaṃprajñāta samādhi arises.

children.text: te khalu nava yogino mṛdumadhyādhimātropāyā bhavanti
children.translated_text: Those yogins are indeed nine, having mild, moderate, or intense means.
That is, one with mild means, one with moderate means, and one with intense means.
Among them, even one with mild means is threefold:
with mild ardor, moderate ardor, or keen ardor.
So too one with moderate means, and so too one with intense means.
Among these, for those whose means are intense,
there is attainment of samādhi and the fruit of samādhi.
There is a further distinction: mildly keen, moderately keen, and intensely keen.

children.text: tadviśeṣān mṛdutīvrasaṃvegasyāsannas tato madhyatīvrasaṃvegasyāsannataras tasmād adhimātratīvrasaṃvegasyādhimātropāyasyāsannatamaḥ samādhilābhaḥ samādhiphalaṃ ceti
children.translated_text: Because of that distinction, attainment of samādhi and the fruit of samādhi are near for one with mildly keen ardor, nearer for one with moderately keen ardor, and nearest for one with intensely keen ardor and intense means.
Does samādhi become nearer only through this?

children.text: athāsya lābhe bhavaty anyo 'pi kaścid upāyo na veti ||
children.translated_text: Or, when it is attained, is there also some other means for this, or not?

children.text: praṇidhānād bhaktiviśeṣād āvarjita īśvaras tam anugṛhṇāty abhidhyānamātreṇa
children.translated_text: Through praṇidhāna, a special devotion, <s>Īśvara</s>, being inclined toward him, favors him by mere contemplation.

children.text: tadabhidhyānamātrād api yogina āsannataraḥ samādhilābhaḥ samādhiphalaṃ ca bhavatīti
children.translated_text: Even from that mere contemplation of him, the yogin's attainment of samādhi and the fruit of samādhi become still nearer.
Now, who is this one called <s>Īśvara</s>, distinct from pradhāna and puruṣa?

children.text: avidyādayaḥ kleśāḥ kuśalākuśalāni karmāṇi tatphalaṃ vipākaḥ tadanuguṇā vāsanā āśayāḥ
children.translated_text: The kleśas, beginning with ignorance, wholesome and unwholesome actions, their fruit, which is ripening, and the latent impressions suited to that fruit, which are deposits:

children.text: te ca manasi vartamānāḥ puruṣe vyapadiśyante sa hi tatphalasya bhokteti
children.translated_text: these, existing in the mind, are attributed to the puruṣa, for he is the experiencer of their fruit.

children.text: yathā jayaḥ parājayo vā yoddhṛṣu vartamānaḥ svāmini vyapadiśyate
children.translated_text: It is like victory or defeat, though existing among the fighters, being attributed to the master.

children.text: yo hy anena bhogenāparāmṛṣṭaḥ sa puruṣaviśeṣa īśvaraḥ
children.translated_text: He who is untouched by this experience is <s>Īśvara</s>, a special puruṣa.

children.text: kaivalyaṃ prāptās tarhi santi ca bahavaḥ kevalinaḥ te hi trīṇi bandhanāni chittvā kaivalyaṃ prāptāḥ
children.translated_text: Then there are many isolated ones who have attained kaivalya, since they have cut the three bonds and attained kaivalya.

children.text: īśvarasya ca tatsaṃbandho na bhūto na bhāvī
children.translated_text: But <s>Īśvara</s> has had no relation to that, nor will he have one.

children.text: yathā muktasya pūrvā bandhakoṭiḥ prajñāyate naivam īśvarasya
children.translated_text: As a prior limit of bondage is known for a liberated person, it is not so for <s>Īśvara</s>.

children.text: yathā vā prakṛtilīnasyottarā bandhakoṭiḥ saṃbhāvyate naivam īśvarasya
children.translated_text: Or as a later limit of bondage is possible for one dissolved in prakṛti, it is not so for <s>Īśvara</s>.

children.text: sa tu sadaiva muktaḥ sadaiveśvara iti
children.translated_text: Rather, he is always liberated and always <s>Īśvara</s>.

children.text: yo 'sau prakṛṣṭasattvopādānād īśvarasya śāśvatika utkarṣaḥ sa kiṃ sanimitta āhosvin nirnimitta iti
children.translated_text: That eternal excellence of <s>Īśvara</s> which comes from the assumption of supreme sattva: does it have a cause, or is it without cause?
Scripture is its cause.
And what is the cause of scripture?
Supreme sattva is its cause.

children.text: etayoḥ śāstrotkarṣayor īśvarasattve vartamānayor anādiḥ saṃbandhaḥ
children.translated_text: Between these two, scripture and excellence, which exist in the reality of <s>Īśvara</s>, there is a beginningless relation.

children.text: etasmād etad bhavati sadaiveśvaraḥ sadaiva mukta iti
children.translated_text: From this it follows that he is always <s>Īśvara</s> and always liberated.

children.text: tac ca tasyaiśvaryaṃ sāmyātiśayavinirmuktam na tāvad aiśvaryāntareṇa tad atiśayyate
children.translated_text: And that sovereignty of his is free from equality and excess; it is not surpassed by any other sovereignty.

children.text: yad evātiśayi syāt tad eva tat syāt
children.translated_text: Whatever would be superior would itself be that.

children.text: tasmād yatra kāṣṭhāprāptir aiśvaryasya sa īśvaraḥ
children.translated_text: Therefore, where sovereignty reaches its utmost limit, that is <s>Īśvara</s>.
Nor is there any sovereignty equal to it.
Why?

children.text: dvayos tulyayor ekasmin yugapat kāmite 'rthe navam idam astu purāṇam idam astv ity ekasya siddhāv itarasya prākāmyavidhātād ūnatvaṃ prasaktam
children.translated_text: If, when two equal beings simultaneously desire the same object, one says, 'Let this be new,' and the other, 'Let this be old,' then, if one succeeds, inferiority would follow for the other because his power of fulfilling desire would be obstructed.

children.text: dvayośca tulyayor yugapat kāmitārthaprāptir nāsti arthasya viruddhatvāt
children.translated_text: And for two equal beings, simultaneous attainment of the desired object is impossible, because the object is contradictory.

children.text: tasmād yasya sāmyātiśayair nivirmuktam aiśvaryaṃ sa eveśvaraḥ sa puruṣaviśeṣa iti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore he whose sovereignty is free from equals and superiors is alone <s>Īśvara</s>, the special puruṣa.
Moreover:

children.text: yad idam atītānāgatapratyutpannapratyekasamuccayātīndriyagrahaṇam alpaṃ bahv iti sarvajñabījam etad vivardhamānaṃ yatra niratiśayaṃ sa sarvajñaḥ
children.translated_text: This grasping of the past, future, and present, whether taken individually or collectively, and of what is beyond the senses, as little or much: this is the seed of omniscience. Where it becomes unsurpassed as it increases, that one is omniscient.

children.text: asti kāṣṭhāprāptiḥ sarvajñabījasya sātiśayatvāt parimāṇavad iti
children.translated_text: There is attainment of the utmost limit of the seed of omniscience, because it admits of degrees, like a measure.
Where knowledge reaches its utmost limit, that one is omniscient.
And he is the special puruṣa.

children.text: sāmānyamātropasaṃhāre ca kṛtopakṣayam anumānaṃ na viśeṣapratipattau samartham iti tasya saṃjñādiviśeṣapratipattir āgamataḥ paryanveṣyā
children.translated_text: And when only the general feature has been gathered, inference, whose force has been spent, is not capable of apprehending the particular. Therefore the apprehension of its particular designation and so on must be sought from authoritative teaching.

children.text: tasyātmānugrahābhāve 'pi bhūtānugrahaḥ prayojanam jñānadharmopadeśena kalpapralayamahāpralayeṣu saṃsāriṇaḥ puruṣān uddhariṣyāmi iti
children.translated_text: Even though there is no benefit for himself, the benefit of beings is his purpose: "By teaching knowledge and <s>dharma</s> I shall lift up the puruṣas who transmigrate during cosmic dissolutions and great dissolutions."
And so it has been said:

children.text: ādividvān nirmāṇacittam adhiṣṭhāya kāruṇyād bhagavān paramarṣir āsuraye jijñāsamānāya tantraṃ provāceti ||
children.translated_text: "The first knower, the blessed supreme seer, having assumed a created mind out of compassion, taught the system to <s>Āsuri</s>, who wished to know."
This is that one.
For former teachers are limited by time.

children.text: yatrāvacchedārthena kālo nopāvartate sa eṣa pūrveṣām api guruḥ
children.translated_text: Where time does not operate so as to impose a limit, this one is the teacher even of the former ones.

children.text: yathāsya sargasyādau prakarṣagatyā siddhas tathātikrāntasargādiṣv api pratyetavyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Just as he is established at the beginning of this creation by the excellence of his course, so he should also be understood in the beginnings of past creations.
<s>Īśvara</s> is the thing signified by praṇava.

children.text: kim asya saṃketakṛtaṃ vācyavācakatvam atha pradīpaprakāśavad avasthitam iti
children.translated_text: Is the relation of signifier and signified in his case made by convention, or is it established like the light of a lamp?
The relation of this signified object with its signifier is established.

children.text: saṃketas tv īśvarasya sthitam evārtham abhinayati
children.translated_text: Convention, however, merely makes manifest the already established object of <s>Īśvara</s>.

children.text: yathāvasthitaḥ pitāputrayoḥ saṃbandhaḥ saṃketenāvadyotyate ayam asya pitā ayam asya putra iti sargāntareṣv api vācyavācakaśaktyapekṣas tathaiva saṃketaḥ kriyate
children.translated_text: Just as the established relation between father and son is illuminated by convention, "This is his father; this is his son," so too in other creations the convention is made in dependence on the power of signified and signifier.

children.text: saṃpratipattinityatayā nityaḥ śabdārthasaṃbandha ity āgaminaḥ pratijānate ||
children.translated_text: The followers of scripture maintain that the relation between word and meaning is eternal because recognition of it is permanent.
For the yogin who has understood the relation of signified and signifier:
there is repetition of praṇava and contemplation of <s>Īśvara</s>, who is denoted by praṇava.

children.text: tad asya yoginaḥ praṇavaṃ japataḥ praṇavārthaṃ ca bhāvayataścittam ekāgraṃ saṃpadyate
children.translated_text: Thus, for this yogin who repeats praṇava and contemplates the meaning of praṇava, the mind becomes one-pointed.
And so it has been said:
"Through study-recitation one should sit in yoga;
through yoga one should engage in study-recitation.
Through the perfection of study-recitation and yoga,
the supreme self becomes manifest."
And what comes about for him from this?

children.text: ye tāvad antarāyā vyādhiprabhṛtayaḥ te tāvad īśvarapraṇidhānān na bhavanti
children.translated_text: Those obstacles, beginning with disease, do not arise because of devotion to <s>Īśvara</s>.
He also comes to see his own nature.

children.text: yathaiveśvaraḥ puruṣaḥ śuddhaḥ prasannaḥ kevalo 'nupasargas tathāyam api buddheḥ pratisaṃvedī yaḥ puruṣaḥ ity evam adhigacchati
children.translated_text: He understands thus: just as <s>Īśvara</s> is a puruṣa, pure, clear, isolated, and free from affliction, so too is this puruṣa who is the witness of the intellect.

children.text: atha ke 'ntarāyāḥ ye cittasya vikṣepāḥ ke punas te kiyanto veti ||
children.translated_text: Now, what are the obstacles that are distractions of the mind? And what, again, are they, and how many are there?
The nine obstacles are distractions of the mind, and these occur together with the mental fluctuations.

children.text: eteṣām abhāve na bhavanti pūrvoktāś cittavṛttayaḥ
children.translated_text: When these are absent, the previously stated mental fluctuations do not occur.
Among them, disease is an imbalance of the bodily elements, fluids, and organs.
Languor is the mind's incapacity for action.

children.text: saṃśayaḥ ubhayakoṭispṛgvijñānaṃ syād idam evaṃ naivaṃ syād iti
children.translated_text: Doubt is cognition touching both alternatives: "Perhaps this is so; perhaps it is not so."
Carelessness is the failure to cultivate the means to samādhi.

children.text: ālasyaṃ kāyasya cittasya ca gurutvād apravṛttiḥ
children.translated_text: Laziness is non-engagement because of heaviness of body and mind.
Non-abstinence is the mind's greed, whose nature is contact with sense-objects.
Erroneous perception is false knowledge.
Failure to attain a stage is non-attainment of a stage of samādhi.
Instability is the mind's failure to become established in a stage that has been attained.

children.text: samādhipratilambhe hi sati tadavasthitaṃ syād iti
children.translated_text: For, when samādhi has been attained, the mind should remain established in that state.

children.text: ete cittavikṣepā nava yogamalā yogapratipakṣā yogāntarāyā ity abhidhīyante ||
children.translated_text: These nine distractions of the mind are called impurities of yoga, opponents of yoga, and obstacles to yoga.
Pain is internal, caused by beings, and caused by divine forces.

children.text: yenābhihatāḥ prāṇinas tadupaghātāya prayatante tad duḥkham
children.translated_text: That by which living beings, when struck, strive to remove that injury is pain.
Depression is the disturbance of the mind caused by obstruction of desire.

children.text: yad aṅgāny ejayati kampayati tad aṅgamejayatvam
children.translated_text: That which shakes and makes the limbs tremble is trembling of the limbs.

children.text: prāṇo yad bāhyaṃ vāyum ācāmati sa śvāsaḥ
children.translated_text: When the vital breath draws in external air, that is inhalation.
When it expels what is in the abdomen, that is exhalation.
These are concomitants of distraction; they occur in one whose mind is distracted.
They do not occur in one whose mind is concentrated.

children.text: athaite vikṣepāḥ samādhipratipakṣās tābhyām evābhyāsavairāgyābhyāṃ niroddhavyāḥ tatrābhyāsasya viṣayam upasaṃharann idam āha ||
children.translated_text: Now, since these distractions are opponents of samādhi, they are to be restrained precisely by practice and dispassion. In this regard, while summing up the object of practice, he says this:
For the sake of preventing distractions, the mind should practice taking support in one reality.

children.text: yasya tu pratyarthaniyataṃ pratyayamātraṃ kṣaṇikaṃ ca cittaṃ tasya sarvam eva cittam ekāgraṃ nāsty eva vikṣiptam
children.translated_text: But for one who holds that the mind is merely a momentary cognition fixed to each separate object, every mind is one-pointed, and none at all is distracted.

children.text: yadi punar idaṃ sarvataḥ pratyāhṛtyaikasminn arthe samādhīyate tadā bhavaty ekāgram ity ato na pratyarthaniyatam
children.translated_text: If, however, this mind, having been withdrawn from all sides, is concentrated on a single object, then it becomes one-pointed; therefore it is not fixed to each separate object.

children.text: yo 'pi sadṛśapratyayapravāhena cittam ekāgraṃ manyate tasyaikāgratā yadi pravāhacittasya dharmas tadaikaṃ nāsti pravāhacittaṃ kṣaṇikatvāt
children.translated_text: And if someone thinks the mind is one-pointed because of a stream of similar cognitions, then, if one-pointedness is a property of the stream-mind, there is no single stream-mind, since it is momentary.
But if it is a property only of the cognition that is a part of the stream,

children.text: sa sarvaḥ sadṛśapratyayapravāhī vā visadṛśapratyayapravāhī vā pratyarthaniyatatvād ekāgra eveti vikṣiptacittānupapattiḥ
children.translated_text: then every such cognition, whether flowing in a stream of similar cognitions or in a stream of dissimilar cognitions, is one-pointed because it is fixed to its own object; thus the existence of a distracted mind would be impossible.

children.text: tasmād ekam anekārtham avasthitaṃ cittam iti
children.translated_text: Therefore the mind is one, has many objects, and is enduring.

children.text: yadi ca cittenaikenānanvitāḥ svabhāvabhinnāḥ pratyayā jāyerann atha katham anyapratyayadṛṣṭasyānyaḥ smartā bhavet anyapratyayopacitasya ca karmāśayasyānyaḥ pratyaya upabhoktā bhavet
children.translated_text: And if cognitions, unconnected by one mind and different by nature, were to arise, then how could one cognition be the rememberer of what was seen by another cognition? And how could another cognition be the experiencer of the karmic deposit accumulated by another cognition?

children.text: kathaṃcit samādhīyamānam apy etad gomayapāyasīyanyāyam ākṣipati
children.translated_text: Even though this is somehow being brought into concentration, it raises the objection of the maxim of cow-dung and milk.
Moreover, if the mind were other in each case, denial of the experience of one's own self would result for the mind.
How so?

children.text: yad aham adrākṣaṃ tat spṛśāmi yac cāsprākṣaṃ tat paśyāmy aham iti pratyayaḥ sarvasya pratyayasya bhede sati pratyayiny abhedenopasthitaḥ
children.translated_text: The cognition, 'What I saw, that I touch, and what I touched, that I see,' when every cognition is different, presents the cognizer as not different.

children.text: ekapratyayaviṣayo 'yam abhedātmāham iti pratyayaḥ katham atyantabhinneṣu citteṣu vartamānaṃ sāmānyam ekaṃ pratyayinam āśrayet
children.translated_text: This cognition 'I,' whose nature is nondifference and which is the object of a single cognition: how could a single generality, existing in utterly different minds, rest upon one cognizer?
And this cognition 'I,' whose nature is nondifference, is grasped by one's own experience.
Nor is the force of perception overpowered by another means of valid knowledge.
And another means of valid knowledge obtains practical operation only through the strength of perception.

children.text: tasmād ekam anekārtham avasthitaṃ ca cittam
children.translated_text: Therefore the mind is one, has many objects, and is established as persistent.

children.text: yasya cittasya avasthitasyedaṃ śāstreṇa parikarma nirdiśyate tat katham ||
children.translated_text: For that mind, being established, this refinement is taught by the śāstra. How is that?

children.text: tatra sarvaprāṇiṣu sukhasaṃbhogāpanneṣu maitrīṃ bhāvayet duḥkhiteṣu karuṇām puṇyātmakeṣu muditām apuṇyaśīleṣūpekṣām
children.translated_text: In that connection, toward all living beings who have come into the enjoyment of happiness one should cultivate friendliness; toward those in pain, compassion; toward those whose nature is merit, joy; and toward those of unmeritorious conduct, equanimity.

children.text: evam asya bhāvayataḥ śuklo dharma upajāyate
children.translated_text: As he cultivates in this way, bright <s>dharma</s> arises in him.

children.text: tataśca cittaṃ prasīdati prasannam ekāgraṃ sthitipadaṃ labhate ||
children.translated_text: And from that the mind becomes clear; being clear, it attains the state of one-pointed steadiness.

children.text: koṣṭhyasya vāyor nāsikāpuṭābhyāṃ prayatnaviśeṣād vamanaṃ pracchardanam
children.translated_text: The expulsion, by a special effort, of the abdominal wind through the nostrils is pracchardana, exhalation.
Holding it is prāṇāyāma (breath control).
Or by those two one should accomplish steadiness of the mind.

children.text: nāsikāgre dhārayato 'sya yā divyagandhasaṃvit sā gandhapravṛttiḥ jihvāgre rasasaṃvit tāluni rūpasaṃvit jihvāmadhye sparśasaṃvit jihvāmūle śabdasaṃvid ity etāḥ vṛttaya utpannāścittaṃ sthitau nibadhnanti saṃśayaṃ vidhamanti samādhiprajñāyāṃ ca dvārībhavantīti
children.translated_text: For one who fixes attention on the tip of the nose, the cognition of divine smell is the activity relating to smell; at the tip of the tongue there is cognition of taste; on the palate, cognition of form; in the middle of the tongue, cognition of touch; at the root of the tongue, cognition of sound. These activities, when arisen, bind the mind in steadiness, dispel doubt, and become gateways to the wisdom of samādhi.

children.text: etena candrādityagrahamaṇipradīparaśmyādiṣu pravṛttir utpannā viṣayavaty eva veditavyā
children.translated_text: By this, an activity that has arisen with regard to moon, sun, planet, jewel, lamp, rays, and the like should likewise be understood as having an object.

children.text: yady api hi tattacchāstrānumānācāryopadeśair avagatam arthatattvaṃ sadbhūtam eva bhavati eteṣāṃ yathābhūtārthapratipādanasāmarthyāt tathāpi yāvad ekadeśo 'pi kaścin na svakaraṇasaṃvedyo bhavati tāvat sarvaṃ parokṣam ivāpavargādiṣu sūkṣmeṣv artheṣu na dṛḍhāṃ buddhim utpādayati
children.translated_text: For even though the reality of a thing, learned from the respective śāstras, inference, and the teacher's instruction, is indeed real, because these are capable of teaching the object as it really is, nevertheless, so long as even some one part is not directly experienced by one's own faculty, everything, as if remote, does not produce firm understanding with regard to subtle objects such as liberation.

children.text: tasmācchāstrānumānācāryopadeśopodbalanārtham evāvaśyaṃ kaścid viśeṣaḥ pratyakṣīkartavyaḥ tatra sadupadiṣṭārthaikadeśapratyakṣatve sati sarvaṃ susūkṣmaviṣayam apy āpavargāt śraddhīyate
children.translated_text: Therefore, precisely in order to strengthen śāstra, inference, and the teacher's instruction, some particular thing must necessarily be made perceptible. When one part of the matter rightly taught has been directly perceived, everything, even what has a very subtle object, is trusted as far as liberation.

children.text: etadartham evedaṃ cittaparikarma nirdiśyate aniyatāsu vṛttiṣu tadviṣayāyāṃ vaśīkārasaṃjñāyām upajātāyāṃ tathā ca sati śraddhāvīryasmṛtisamādhayo 'syāpratibandhena bhaviṣyantīti ||
children.translated_text: For this very purpose this refinement of the mind is taught: when mastery, so called, has arisen over its object among the unsteady activities, then faith, energy, mindfulness, and samādhi will occur for him without obstruction.
The phrase 'an activity that has arisen binds the mind in steadiness' is to be carried forward.

children.text: hṛdayapuṇḍarīke dhārayato yā buddhisaṃvit buddhisattvaṃ hi bhāsvaram ākāśakalpam tatra sthitivaiśāradyāt
children.translated_text: For one who fixes attention on the lotus of the heart, the cognition of the intellect arises; for the sattva of the intellect is luminous, like space, because of expert steadiness there.

children.text: tathāsmitāyāṃ samāpannaṃ cittaṃ nistaraṃgamahodadhikalpaṃ śāntam anantam asmitāmātraṃ bhavati
children.translated_text: Likewise, the mind absorbed in asmitā (I-am-ness) becomes like a great ocean without waves, peaceful, infinite, consisting only of asmitā.
In this connection it has been said:

children.text: tam aṇumātram ātmānam anuvidyāsmīty evaṃ tāvat samprajānīte iti
children.translated_text: 'Having understood that self, minute in measure, one then knows only thus: I am.'

children.text: eṣā dvayī viśokā viṣayavatī asmitāmātrā ca pravṛttir jyotiṣmatīty ucyate yayā yoginaścittaṃ sthitipadaṃ labhata iti ||
children.translated_text: This twofold activity, free from sorrow, both having an object and consisting only of asmitā, is called luminous; by it the yogin's mind attains the state of steadiness.

children.text: vītarāgacittālambanoparaktaṃ vā yoginaścittaṃ sthitipadaṃ labhata iti ||
children.translated_text: Or the yogin's mind, colored by taking as its support the mind of one free from passion, attains the state of steadiness.

children.text: svapnajñānālambanaṃ vā nidrājñānālambanaṃ vā tadākāraṃ yoginaścittaṃ sthitipadaṃ labhata iti ||
children.translated_text: Or the yogin's mind, taking as support knowledge from dream or knowledge from sleep, and assuming that form, attains the state of steadiness.
Whatever is desired, just that should be meditated upon.

children.text: tatra labdhasthitikam anyatrāpi sthitipadaṃ labhata iti ||
children.translated_text: Having acquired steadiness there, it attains the state of steadiness elsewhere also.

children.text: sūkṣme niviśamānasya paramāṇvantaṃ sthitipadaṃ labhata iti
children.translated_text: For one entering into the subtle, the mind attains the state of steadiness extending as far as the atom.
For one entering into the gross, the state of steadiness of the mind extends as far as the supreme greatness.

children.text: evaṃ tām ubhayīṃ koṭim anudhāvato yo 'syāpratīghātaḥ sa paro vaśīkāraḥ
children.translated_text: When it runs along both of these limits in this way, the absence of obstruction for it is the higher mastery.

children.text: tadvaśīkārāt paripūrṇaṃ yoginaścittaṃ na punar abhyāsakṛtaṃ parikarmāpekṣata iti
children.translated_text: Through that mastery, the yogin's mind, being complete, no longer depends on refinement produced by practice.

children.text: atha labdhasthitikasya cetasaḥ kiṃsvarūpā kiṃviṣayā vā samāpattir iti
children.translated_text: Now, for the mind that has acquired steadiness, what is the nature of samāpatti, and what is its object?
This is stated:
'Of one whose activities have diminished' means 'of one whose cognitions have subsided.'
'Like a well-born jewel' is the statement of an example.

children.text: yathā sphaṭika upāśrayabhedāt tattadrūpoparakta upāśrayarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsate tathā grāhyālambanoparaktaṃ cittaṃ grāhyasamāpannaṃ grāhyasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsate
children.translated_text: Just as crystal, because of the difference in its support, is colored by this or that form and shines forth in the form and appearance of the support, so the mind, colored by the support that is the grasped object and absorbed in the grasped object, shines forth in the form and appearance of the grasped object's own nature.
Likewise, when colored by the subtle elements and absorbed in the subtle elements, it has the appearance of the own nature of the subtle elements.

children.text: tathā sthūlālambanoparaktaṃ sthūlarūpasamāpannaṃ sthūlarūpābhāsaṃ bhavati tathā viśvabhedoparaktaṃ viśvabhedasamāpannaṃ viśvarūpābhāsaṃ bhavati
children.translated_text: Likewise, colored by a gross support, having entered into a gross form, it appears with a gross form; and likewise, colored by the divisions of the whole world, having entered into the divisions of the whole world, it appears with a universal form.
The same is to be understood also in the instruments of grasping, the senses.
Colored by the support that is grasping, having entered into grasping, it shines forth in the form and shape of grasping.
Likewise, colored by the support that is the grasping puruṣa, having entered into the grasping puruṣa, it shines forth in the form and shape of the grasping puruṣa.

children.text: tathā muktapuruṣālambanoparaktaṃ muktapuruṣasamāpannaṃ muktapuruṣasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsata iti
children.translated_text: Likewise, colored by the support that is a liberated puruṣa, having entered into the liberated puruṣa, it shines forth in the form and shape of the liberated puruṣa.

children.text: tad evam abhijātamaṇikalpasya cetaso grahītṛgrahaṇagrāhyeṣu puruṣendriyabhūteṣu yā tatsthatadañjanatā teṣu sthitasya tadākārāpattiḥ sā samāpattir ity ucyate ||
children.translated_text: Thus, for a mind like a flawless jewel, the condition of being situated in, and colored by, the grasper, the instrument of grasping, and the grasped, namely puruṣa, sense-organ, and element, while it is situated in them and assumes their form, is called samāpatti.

children.text: tad yathā gaur iti śabdo gaur ity artho gaur iti jñānam ity avibhāgena vibhaktānām api grahaṇaṃ dṛṣṭam
children.translated_text: For example, one observes the apprehension, without division, of what are in fact divided: the word 'cow,' the meaning 'cow,' and the cognition 'cow.'

children.text: vibhajyamānāścānye śabdadharmā anye arthadharmā anye jñānadharmā ity eteṣāṃ vibhaktaḥ panthāḥ
children.translated_text: But when they are analyzed, the properties of word are different, the properties of meaning are different, and the properties of cognition are different; thus the path of these is distinct.

children.text: tatra samāpannasya yogino yo gavādyarthaḥ samādhiprajñāyāṃ samārūḍhaḥ sa cec chabdārthajñānavikalpānuviddha upāvartate sā saṃkīrṇā samāpattiḥ savitarkety ucyate
children.translated_text: In that case, if for the yogin who has entered samāpatti the object, such as a cow, has ascended into the wisdom of samādhi, and if it turns back accompanied by conceptual construction concerning word, meaning, and cognition, that mixed samāpatti is called savitarka.

children.text: yadā punaḥ śabdasaṃketasmṛtipariśuddhau śrutānumānajñānavikalpaśūnyāyāṃ samādhiprajñāyāṃ svarūpamātreṇāvasthito 'rthas tatsvarūpākāramātratayaivāvacchidyate sā ca nirvitarkā samāpattiḥ
children.translated_text: But when, upon the purification of memory concerning verbal convention, the object stands in the wisdom of samādhi devoid of conceptual constructions from knowledge based on scripture and inference, solely by its own form, and is delimited only as the shape of that very form, that is nirvitarka samāpatti.
That is the supreme direct perception.
And it is the seed of scripture and inference.
From it scripture and inference arise.
And that seeing does not arise together with knowledge from scripture and inference.

children.text: tasmād asaṃkīrṇaṃ pramāṇāntareṇa yogino nirvitarkasamādhijaṃ darśanam iti
children.translated_text: Therefore the yogin's vision born from nirvitarka samādhi is unmixed with any other pramāṇa (means of valid knowledge).

children.text: nirvitarkāyāḥ samāpatter asyāḥ sūtreṇa lakṣaṇaṃ dyotyate ||
children.translated_text: The definition of this nirvitarka samāpatti is indicated by the sūtra.

children.text: yā śabdasaṃketaśrutānumānajñānavikalpasmṛtipariśuddhau grāhyasvarūpoparaktā prajñā svam iva prajñārūpaṃ grahaṇātmakaṃ tyaktvā padārthamātrasvarūpā grāhyasvarūpāpanneva bhavati sā nirvitarkā samāpattiḥ
children.translated_text: When, upon the purification of memory from verbal convention, scripture, inference, knowledge, and conceptual construction, wisdom colored by the own form of the grasped object abandons, as it were, its own form as wisdom, which has the nature of grasping, and has the form of the object alone, as though it had entered into the own form of the grasped object, that is nirvitarka samāpatti.
And this has been explained as follows.

children.text: tasyā ekabuddhyupakramo hy arthātmāṇupracayaviśesātmā gavādir ghaṭādir vā lokaḥ
children.translated_text: For the object-reality, such as a cow or a pot, which is grasped by the initiation of a single cognition, is the world whose nature is a particular aggregation of atoms.

children.text: sa ca saṃsthānaviśeṣo bhūtasūkṣmāṇāṃ sādhāraṇo dharma ātmabhūtaḥ phalena vyaktenānumitaḥ svavyañajkāñjanaḥ prādur bhavati dharmāntarasya kapālāder udaye
children.translated_text: And that particular configuration of subtle elements is a common property, inherent in them, inferred from its manifest effect; when another property, such as the potsherd, arises, it appears as colored by its own manifestors.
This property is called the whole possessing parts.

children.text: yo 'sāv ekaśca mahāṃs cāṇīyāṃśca sparśavāṃśca kriyādharmakaścānityaśca tenāvayavinā vyavahārāḥ kriyante
children.translated_text: Transactions are carried out with that whole possessing parts, which is one and large and smaller, which has touch, has action as its property, and is impermanent.

children.text: yasya punar avastukaḥ sa pracayaviśeṣaḥ sūkṣmaṃ ca kāraṇam anupalabhyam avikalpasya tasyāvayavyabhāvād atadrūpapratiṣṭhaṃ mithyājñānam iti prāyeṇa sarvam eva prāptaṃ mithyājñānam iti
children.translated_text: But for one for whom that particular aggregation is without real substance, and the subtle cause is imperceptible, because there is no whole possessing parts for one without conceptual construction, cognition established in a form other than that would be false cognition; thus almost everything would become false cognition.

children.text: tadā ca samyagjñānam api kiṃ syād viṣayābhāvāt
children.translated_text: And in that case what could right knowledge be, since there would be no object?

children.text: yad yad upalabhyate tat tad avayavitvenāmnātam
children.translated_text: Whatever is apprehended, each such thing is stated as having the character of a whole possessing parts.

children.text: tasmād asty avayavī yo mahattvādivyavahārāpannaḥ samāpatter nirvitarkāyā viṣayo bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Therefore there is a whole possessing parts, which is involved in transactions such as largeness, and which becomes the object of nirvitarka samāpatti.

children.text: tatra bhūtasūkṣmeṣv abhivyaktadharmakeṣu deśakālanimittānubhavāvachinneṣu yā samāpattiḥ sā savicārety ucyate
children.translated_text: Among subtle elements whose properties have become manifest, delimited by place, time, cause, and experience, the samāpatti that occurs there is called savicāra.

children.text: tatrāpy ekabuddhinirgrāhyam evoditadharmaviśiṣṭaṃ bhūtasūkṣmam ālambanībhūtaṃ samādhiprajñāyām upatiṣṭhate
children.translated_text: There too the subtle element, characterized by an arisen property and graspable by a single cognition, stands as the support in the wisdom of samādhi.

children.text: yā punaḥ sarvathā sarvataḥ śāntoditāvyapadeśyadharmān avachinneṣu sarvadharmānupātiṣu sarvadharmātmakeṣu samāpattiḥ sā nirvicārety ucyate
children.translated_text: But the samāpatti that occurs in entities whose properties are in every way, on every side, quiescent, arisen, and indeterminable, and that follow all properties and have the nature of all properties, is called nirvicāra.

children.text: evaṃsvar-paṃ hi tadbhūtasūkṣmam etenaiva svarūpeṇālambanībhūtam eva samādhiprajñāsvarūpam uparañjayati
children.translated_text: For that subtle element is of just such a nature; as the support in precisely this form, it colors the very form of the wisdom of samādhi.

children.text: prajñā ca svarūpaśūnyevārthamātrā yadā bhavati tadā nirvicārety ucyate
children.translated_text: And when wisdom, as though empty of its own form, becomes only the object, then it is called nirvicāra.

children.text: tatra mahadvastuviṣayā savitarkā nirvitarkā ca sūkṣmavastuviṣayā savicārā nirvicārā ca
children.translated_text: There, savitarka and nirvitarka have gross objects as their domain, while savicāra and nirvicāra have subtle objects as their domain.

children.text: evam ubhayor etayaiva nirvitarkayā vikalpahānir vyākhyāteti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, for both, the removal of conceptual construction has been explained by this same nirvitarka samāpatti.

children.text: pārthivasyāṇor gandhatanmātraṃ sūkṣmo viṣayaḥ āpyasya rasatanmātram taijasasya rūpatanmātram vāyavīyasya sparśatanmātram ākāśasya śabdatanmātram iti
children.translated_text: For the earthy atom the subtle object is merely the smell-tanmātra; for the watery, merely the taste-tanmātra; for the fiery, merely the form-tanmātra; for the airy, merely the touch-tanmātra; for space, merely the sound-tanmātra.

children.text: teṣām ahaṃkāraḥ asyāpi liṅgamātraṃ sūkṃso viṣayaḥ
children.translated_text: For those, ahaṃkāra is the subtle object; and for this too, liṅgamātra is the subtle object.
For liṅgamātra also, the aliṅga is the subtle object.
And there is nothing subtler than the aliṅga.
But is not puruṣa subtle?
True.

children.text: yathā liṅgāt param aliṅgasya saukṣmyaṃ na caivaṃ puruṣasya
children.translated_text: Yet just as the aliṅga is subtler than the liṅga, the puruṣa is not so.

children.text: kiṃ tu liṅgasyānvayikāraṇaṃ puruṣo na bhavati hetus tu bhavatīti
children.translated_text: Rather, puruṣa is not the material cause that continues into the liṅga; but it is a cause in the sense of an occasion.
Therefore, unsurpassed subtlety has been explained in pradhāna.
Yoga does not succeed for one who is not an ascetic.

children.text: anādikarmakleśavāsanācitrā pratyupasthitaviṣayajālā cāśuddhir nāntareṇa tapaḥ saṃbhedam āpadyata iti tapasa upādānam ||
children.translated_text: Impurity, variegated by beginningless karma, <s>kleśa</s> (affliction), and latent impressions, and furnished with the net of objects presently appearing, does not undergo rupture without tapas; therefore tapas is adopted.

children.text: tac ca cittaprasādanam abādhyamānam anenāsevyam iti manyate ||
children.translated_text: And one considers that this, the purification of the mind, is to be practiced insofar as it is not obstructed by that.
<s>Svādhyāya</s> is the recitation of purifying formulas such as praṇava, or the study of treatises on liberation.
<s>Īśvarapraṇidhāna</s> is the offering of all actions to the supreme guru.
Or it is the renunciation of their fruit.
That indeed is <s>kriyāyoga</s>.
For when it is practiced, it develops samādhi.
And it attenuates the <s>kleśas</s>.

children.text: pratanūkṛtān kleśān prasaṃkhyānāgninā dagdhabījakalpān aprasavadharmiṇaḥ kariṣyatīti teṣāṃ tanūkaraṇāt punaḥ kleśair aparāmṛṣṭā sattvapuruṣānyatāmātrakhyātiḥ sūkṣmā prajñā samāptādhikārā pratiprasavāya kalpayiṣyata iti ||
children.translated_text: Having attenuated the <s>kleśas</s>, it will make them like seeds burned by the fire of discriminative knowledge, no longer having the nature of producing offspring; and because they are attenuated, a subtle wisdom, consisting solely in the discernment of the difference between sattva and <s>puruṣa</s>, untouched thereafter by the <s>kleśas</s> and having completed its task, will be made fit for reabsorption.
Now, what are the <s>kleśas</s>, and how many are they?

children.text: kleśā iti pañca viparyayā ity arthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The word '<s>kleśas</s>' means the five misapprehensions.

children.text: te spandamānā guṇādhikāraṃ draḍhayanti pariṇāmam avasthāpayanti kāryakāraṇasrota unnamayanti parasparānugrahatantrībhūtvā karmavipākaṃ cābhinirharantīti ||
children.translated_text: When they are active, they strengthen the authority of the guṇas, establish transformation, raise up the stream of cause and effect, and, having become dependent on mutual assistance, bring forth the ripening of karma.

children.text: atrāvidyā kṣetraṃ prasavabhūmir uttareṣām asmitādīnāṃ caturvidhavikalpānāṃ prasuptatanuvicchinnodārāṇām ||
children.translated_text: Here <s>avidyā</s> is the field, the breeding ground, for the fourfold alternatives beginning with asmitā and the others: dormant, attenuated, interrupted, and fully active.
Among these, what is dormancy?
It is the assumption of seed-state by those that are established in the mind merely as potencies.
Their awakening is their coming face to face with an object.

children.text: prasaṃkhyānavato dagdhakleśabījasya saṃmukhībhūte 'py ālambane nāsau punar asti dagdhabījasya kutaḥ praroha iti ataḥ kṣīṇakleśaḥ kuśalaścaramadeha ity ucyate ||
children.translated_text: For one who possesses discriminative knowledge, whose seeds of <s>kleśa</s> have been burned, that <s>kleśa</s> no longer exists even when the object comes face to face; how could there be a sprout from a burned seed? Therefore one whose <s>kleśas</s> are exhausted, who is skillful and has a final body, is so called.

children.text: tatraiva sā dagdhabījabhāvā pañcamī kleśāvasthā nānyatreti ||
children.translated_text: Only there is that fifth state of <s>kleśa</s>, the condition of a burned seed, and nowhere else.

children.text: satāṃ kleśānāṃ tadā bījasāmarthyaṃ dagdham iti ||
children.translated_text: At that time, although the <s>kleśas</s> exist, their seed-capacity has been burned.

children.text: viṣayasya saṃmukhībhāve 'pi sati na bhavaty eṣāṃ prabodha iti uktā prasuptiḥ dagdhabījānām aprarohaśca ||
children.translated_text: Even when the object is present face to face, there is no awakening of them; thus dormancy has been stated, and also the non-sprouting of burned seeds.

children.text: tanutvam ucyate pratipakṣabhāvanopahatāḥ kleśās tanavo bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: Attenuation is now stated: the <s>kleśas</s>, struck down by the cultivation of their opposites, become thin.

children.text: tathā vicchidya vicchidya tena tenātmanā punaḥ punaḥ samudācaranti iti vicchinnāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, when they arise again and again in this or that form after repeated interruption, they are called interrupted.
How so?

children.text: rāgakāle krodhasyādarśanāt na hi rāgakāle krodhaḥ samudācarati ||
children.translated_text: Because anger is not seen at the time of passion; for anger does not arise at the time of passion.

children.text: rāgaśca kvacid dṛśyamāno na viṣayāntare nāsti ||
children.translated_text: And passion, though seen somewhere, is not absent with respect to another object.

children.text: naikasyāṃ striyāṃ caitro rakta ity anyāsu strīṣu viraktaḥ kiṃtu tatra rāgo labdhavṛttir anyatra tu bhaviṣyadvṛttir iti ||
children.translated_text: It is not that because <s>Caitra</s> is passionately attached to one woman he is dispassionate toward other women; rather, with regard to her passion has obtained its activity, while elsewhere it has a future activity.
For at that time it is dormant, attenuated, and interrupted.
That which has obtained activity with regard to an object is fully active.
All these, indeed, do not pass beyond the condition of having the <s>kleśas</s> as their domain.

children.text: kas tarhi vicchinnaḥ prasuptas tanur udāro vā kleśa iti ||
children.translated_text: Then which <s>kleśa</s> is interrupted, dormant, attenuated, or fully active?
It is answered: this is certainly true.
But these conditions of being interrupted and so on belong only to them when they are particularized.

children.text: yathaiva pratipakṣabhāvanāto vivṛttas tathaiva svavyañjakāñjanenābhivyakta iti ||
children.translated_text: Just as it is turned back by cultivating the opposite, so too it is manifested by the collyrium that reveals it.
All these <s>kleśas</s> are varieties of <s>avidyā</s>.
Why?
In all of them <s>avidyā</s> alone overflows.

children.text: yad avidyayā vastv ākāryate tad evānuśerate kleśā viparyāsapratyayakāla upalabhyante kṣīyamāṇāṃ cāvidyām anukṣīyanta iti ||
children.translated_text: Whatever object is shaped by <s>avidyā</s>, the <s>kleśas</s> lie latent in that very thing; they are perceived at the time of erroneous cognition, and when <s>avidyā</s> is being diminished, they too diminish along with it.
There the nature of <s>avidyā</s> is stated.
In what is impermanent and produced, there is the cognition of permanence.

children.text: tad yathā dhruvā pṛthivī dhruvā sacandratārakā dyauḥ amṛtā divaukasa iti ||
children.translated_text: For example: 'The earth is firm, the heaven with moon and stars is firm, the gods are immortal.'
Likewise, in the impure and utterly repulsive body, there is the cognition of purity.
And it has been said:

children.text: sthānād bījād upaṣṭambhān niḥsyandān nidhanād api ||
children.translated_text: From its place, from its seed, from its support, from its outflow, and even from its destruction,

children.text: kāyam ādheyaśaucatvāt paṇḍitā hy aśuciṃ viduḥ ||
children.translated_text: because the body has purity only as something imposed, the wise know it to be impure.
Thus the cognition of purity is seen in what is impure.

children.text: naveva śaśāṅkalekhā kamanīyeyaṃ kanyā madhvamṛtāvayavanirmiteva candraṃ bhittvā niḥsṛteva jñāyate nīlotpalapatrāyatākṣī hāvagarbhābhyāṃ locanābhyāṃ jīvalokam āśvāsayantīveti kasya kenābhisaṃbandhaḥ bhavati caivam aśucau śuciviparyāsapratyaya iti ||
children.translated_text: 'This maiden is lovely like a new digit of the moon, as if formed of honey and nectar, as if she had broken through the moon and emerged; with eyes long like blue-lotus petals, and with glances full of dalliance, she seems to console the world of living beings.' What connection has anything here with anything else? Yet in this way an erroneous cognition of purity occurs in what is impure.
By this, the notion of merit in what is demerit, and likewise the notion of benefit in what is harmful, have been explained.
Likewise, he will state the cognition of pleasure in what is pain:

children.text: pariṇāmatāpasaṃskāraduḥkhair guṇavṛttivirodhācca duḥkham eva sarvaṃ vivekinaḥ iti ||
children.translated_text: 'For the discerning one, all is nothing but pain, because of the pains of transformation, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the opposition among the activities of the guṇas.'
There the cognition of pleasure is <s>avidyā</s>.

children.text: tathānātmany ātmakhyātir bāhyopakaraṇeṣu cetanācetaneṣu bhogādhiṣṭhāne vā śarīre puruṣopakaraṇe vā manasy anātmany ātmakhyātir iti ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, the cognition of self in what is not self: in external instruments, whether conscious or unconscious, or in the body as the locus of enjoyment, or in the mind as an instrument of <s>puruṣa</s>, there is the cognition of self in what is not self.
Thus this is said here.

children.text: vyaktam avyaktaṃ vā sattvam ātmatvenābhipratītya tasya saṃpadam anunandaty ātmasaṃpadaṃ manvānas tasya vyāpadam anuśocaty ātmavyāpadaṃ manyamānaḥ sa sarvo 'pratibuddha iti ||
children.translated_text: Having taken manifest or unmanifest sattva as the self, he rejoices in its prosperity, thinking it to be the prosperity of the self; and he grieves over its injury, thinking it to be the injury of the self. All such a person is unawakened.

children.text: eṣā catuṣpadā bhavaty avidyā mūlam asya kleśasaṃtānasya karmāśayasya ca savipākasyeti ||
children.translated_text: This ignorance has four feet; it is the root of this continuum of kleśas and of the karmic deposit together with its fruition.
And its real nature is to be understood as a positive entity, like 'non-friend' and 'non-cow-track.'

children.text: yathā nāmitro mitrābhāvo na mitramātraṃ kiṃtu tadviruddhaḥ sapatnaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For just as a 'non-friend' is not the absence of a friend, nor merely a friend, but an enemy opposed to him,

children.text: tathāgoṣpadaṃ na goṣpadābhāvo na goṣpadamātraṃ kiṃtu deśa eva tābhyām anyad vastvantaram ||
children.translated_text: so a 'non-cow-track' is not the absence of a cow-track, nor merely a cow-track, but a place itself, another real thing different from both of them.

children.text: evam avidyā na pramāṇaṃ na pramāṇābhāvaḥ kiṃtu vidyāviparītaṃ jñānāntaram avidyeti ||
children.translated_text: In the same way, ignorance is not valid cognition and not the absence of valid cognition, but another cognition contrary to knowledge; that is ignorance.

children.text: puruṣo dṛkśaktir buddhir darśanaśaktir ity etayor ekasvarūpāpattir ivāsmitā kleśa ucyate ||
children.translated_text: The puruṣa is the power of seeing, and the intellect is the power of vision; the apparent coming into one nature of these two is called the kleśa of asmitā.

children.text: bhoktṛbhogyaśaktyor atyantavibhaktayor atyantāsaṃkīrṇayor avibhāgaprāptāviva satyāṃ bhogaḥ kalpate svarūpapratilambhe tu tayoḥ kaivalyam eva bhavati kuto bhoga iti ||
children.translated_text: Experience is imagined when the powers of experiencer and experienced, though utterly distinct and utterly unmixed, have as it were attained non-separation. But when they regain their own nature, there is only kaivalya for the two; how could there be experience?

children.text: buddhitaḥ paraṃ puruṣam ākāraśīlavidyādibhir vibhaktam apaśyan kuryāt tatrātmabuddhiṃ mohena iti ||
children.translated_text: Not seeing the puruṣa as beyond the intellect and distinct from it by form, character, knowledge, and the like, one would, through delusion, form the notion of self there.

children.text: sukhābhijñasya sukhānusmṛtipūrvaḥ sukhe tatsādhane vā yo gardhas tṛṣṇā lobhaḥ sa rāga iti ||
children.translated_text: For one who has known pleasure, the craving, thirst, or greed for pleasure or for its means, preceded by the memory of pleasure, is rāga.

children.text: duḥkhābhijñasya duḥkhānusmṛtipūrvo duḥkhe tatsādhane vā yaḥ pratigho manyur jighāṃsā krodhaḥ sa dveṣa iti ||
children.translated_text: For one who has known pain, the resistance, resentment, desire to harm, or anger toward pain or toward its means, preceded by the memory of pain, is dveṣa.

children.text: sarvasya prāṇina iyam ātmāśir nityā bhavati mā na bhūvaṃ bhūyāsam iti ||
children.translated_text: In every living being this eternal self-wish exists: 'May I not cease to be; may I continue to be.'
And this self-wish does not belong to one whose nature of death has never been experienced.
By this, experience in a former birth is inferred.

children.text: kṛmer api jātamātrasya pratyakṣānumānāgamair asaṃbhāvito maraṇatrāsa ucchedadṛṣṭyātmakaḥ pūrvajanmānubhūtaṃ maraṇaduḥkham anumāpayati ||
children.translated_text: Even in a worm just born, the fear of death, not accounted for by perception, inference, or testimony and having the nature of a view of annihilation, leads one to infer the pain of death experienced in a previous birth.

children.text: yathā cāyam atyantamūḍheṣu dṛśyate kleśas tathā viduṣo 'pi vijñātapūrvāparāntasya rūḍhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And just as this kleśa is seen among the extremely deluded, so it is also ingrained in the learned person who knows the prior and later limits.
Why?

children.text: samānā hi tayoḥ kuśalākuśalayor maraṇaduḥkhānubhavād iyaṃ vāsaneti ||
children.translated_text: For in both, the skilled and the unskilled, this latent impression is the same because of the experience of the pain of death.

children.text: te pañca kleśā dagdhabījakalpā yoginaścaritādhikāre cetasi pralīne saha tenaivāstaṃ gacchanti ||
children.translated_text: Those five kleśas, like burnt seeds, pass away together with the mind itself when, for the yogin whose purpose has been fulfilled, the mind has dissolved.
But for those that remain, having assumed the condition of seeds,

children.text: kleśānāṃ yā vṛttayaḥ sthūlās tāḥ kriyāyogena tanūkṛtāḥ satyaḥ prasaṃkhyānena dhyānena hātavyā yāvat sūkṣmīkṛtā yāvad dagdhabījakalpā iti ||
children.translated_text: the gross activities of the kleśas, once attenuated by kriyāyoga, are to be abandoned by discriminative meditation until they have been made subtle, until they are like burnt seeds.

children.text: yathā vastrāṇāṃ sthūlo malaḥ pūrvaṃ nirdhūyate paścāt sūkṣmo yatnenopāyena vāpanīyate tathā svalpapratipakṣāḥ sthūlā vṛttayaḥ kleśānāṃ sūkṣmās tu mahāpratipakṣā iti ||
children.translated_text: Just as the coarse dirt of cloths is first shaken off, and afterward the fine dirt must be removed by effort or by a method, so the gross activities of the kleśas have a small counteragent, but the subtle ones have a great counteragent.
There, the karmic deposit of merit and demerit arises from desire, greed, delusion, anger, and the like.
It is either to be experienced in the seen birth or to be experienced in an unseen birth.

children.text: tatra tīvrasaṃvegena mantratapaḥsamādhibhir nirvartita īśvaradevatāmaharṣimahānubhāvānām ārādhanād vā yaḥ pariniṣpannaḥ sa sadyaḥ paripacyate puṇyakarmāśaya iti ||
children.translated_text: Among these, the karmic deposit of merit that is accomplished through intense ardor by mantras, austerity, and samādhi, or through the worship of <s>Īśvara</s>, deities, great seers, and great beings, ripens immediately.

children.text: yathā tīvrakleśena bhītavyādhitakṛpaṇeṣu viśvāsopagateṣu vā mahānubhāveṣu vā tapasviṣu kṛtaḥ punaḥ punar apakāraḥ sa cāpi pāpakarmāśayaḥ sadya eva paripacyate yathā nandīśvaraḥ kumāro manuṣyapariṇāmaṃ hitvā devatvena pariṇataḥ tathā nahuṣo 'pi devānām indraḥ svakaṃ pariṇāmaṃ hitvā tiryaktvena pariṇata iti ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, repeated injury done with intense affliction to the frightened, the sick, the miserable, those who have put trust in one, great beings, or ascetics is also a karmic deposit of evil that ripens immediately. Thus <s>Nandīśvara</s> the youth, abandoning the transformation of a human, was transformed into deityhood; and similarly <s>Nahuṣa</s>, the Indra of the gods, abandoning his own transformation, was transformed into an animal condition.
In this matter, for hell-beings there is no karmic deposit to be experienced in the seen birth.
And for those whose kleśas are exhausted, there is no karmic deposit to be experienced in an unseen birth.

children.text: satsu kleśeṣu karmāśayo vipākārambhī bhavati nocchinnakleśamūlaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When the kleśas exist, the karmic deposit begins its fruition; when the root of the kleśas has been cut off, it does not.

children.text: yathā tuṣāvanaddhāḥ śālitaṇḍulā adagdhabījabhāvāḥ prarohasamarthā bhavanti nāpanītatuṣā dagdhabījabhāvā vā tathā kleśāvanaddhaḥ karmāśayo vipākaprarohī bhavati nāpanītakleśo na prasaṃkhyānadagdhakleśabījabhāvo veti ||
children.translated_text: Just as rice grains enclosed in husk, not having the condition of burnt seeds, are capable of sprouting, but not those from which the husk has been removed or those that have the condition of burnt seeds, so a karmic deposit enclosed by kleśas sprouts into fruition, but not one whose kleśas have been removed or whose kleśa-seeds have been burnt by discriminative knowledge.

children.text: sa ca vipākas trividho jātir āyur bhoga iti ||
children.translated_text: And that fruition is threefold: birth, lifespan, and experience.
Here this is to be considered:

children.text: kim ekaṃ karmaikasya janmanaḥ kāraṇam athaikaṃ karmānekaṃ janmākṣipatīti ||
children.translated_text: Is one action the cause of one birth, or does one action bring about many births?

children.text: dvitīyā vicāraṇā kim anekaṃ karmānekaṃ janma nirvartayaty athānekaṃ karmaikaṃ janma nirvartayatīti ||
children.translated_text: A second consideration is this: does many an action produce many births, or does many an action produce one birth?

children.text: na tāvad ekaṃ karmaikasya janmanaḥ kāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: First, one action is not the cause of one birth.
Why?

children.text: anādikālapracitasyāsaṃkhyeyasyāviśiṣṭakarmaṇaḥ sāṃpratikasya ca phalakramāniyamād anāśvāso lokasya prasaktaḥ sa cāniṣṭa iti ||
children.translated_text: Because, owing to the absence of a fixed order of results for action accumulated from beginningless time, innumerable and undifferentiated, and for present action as well, uncertainty for the world would follow; and that is undesirable.
Nor is one action the cause of many births.
Why?

children.text: anekeṣu karmasv ekaikam eva karmānekasya janmanaḥ kāraṇam ity avaśiṣṭasya vipākakālābhāvaḥ prasaktaḥ sa cāpy aniṣṭa iti ||
children.translated_text: If, among many actions, each single action were the cause of many births, then for the remaining actions the absence of a time for fruition would follow; and that too is undesirable.
Nor is many an action the cause of many births.
Why?

children.text: tad anekaṃ janma yugapan na sambhavati iti krameṇaiva vācyam tathā ca pūrvadoṣānuṣaṅgaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because those many births cannot occur simultaneously; therefore they would have to be said to occur in sequence, and in that case the earlier fault follows.

children.text: tasmājjanmaprāyaṇāntare kṛtaḥ puṇyāpuṇyakarmāśayapracayo vicitraḥ pradhānopasarjanabhāvenāvasthitaḥ prāyaṇābhivyakta ekapraghaṭṭakena tac ca janma tenaiva karmaṇā labdhāyuṣkaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Therefore the varied accumulation of karmic deposits of merit and demerit, produced in the interval between birth and death, standing in the relation of principal and subordinate, and manifested at death, operates as a single aggregate; and that birth, by that very action, comes to have a lifespan allotted to it.

children.text: tasminn āyuṣi tenaiva karmaṇā bhogaḥ sampadyata iti ||
children.translated_text: Within that lifespan, experience is accomplished by that same action.
That <s>karmāśaya</s> (karmic deposit), because it is the cause of birth, lifespan, and experience, is said to have threefold fruition.
Hence the <s>karmāśaya</s> has been called one-birth-producing.

children.text: dṛṣṭajanmavedanīyas tv ekavipākārambhī bhogahetutvād dvivipākārambhī vā bhogāyurhetutvān nandīśvaravan nahuṣavad veti ||
children.translated_text: But what is to be experienced in the visible birth begins with one fruition, because it is the cause of experience; or it begins with two fruitions, because it is the cause of experience and lifespan, as in the cases of <s>Nandīśvara</s> and <s>Nahuṣa</s>.

children.text: kleśakarmavipākānubhavanirvartitābhis tu vāsanābhir anādikālasaṃmūrchitam idaṃ cittaṃ vicitrīkṛtam iva sarvato matsyajālaṃ granthibhir ivātatam ity etā anekabhavapūrvikā vāsanāḥ ||
children.translated_text: But this mind, diversified as it were by the latent impressions produced by the experience of kleśas, actions, and their fruitions, and thickened from beginningless time, is spread out on all sides like a fish-net with knots; these latent impressions have many births behind them.

children.text: yas tvayaṃ karmāśaya eṣa evaikabhavika ukta iti ||
children.translated_text: But this <s>karmāśaya</s> here has been described as one-birth-producing.

children.text: ye saṃskārāḥ smṛtihetavas tā vāsanās tāścānādikālīnā iti ||
children.translated_text: The saṃskāras that are causes of memory are the latent impressions, and they are beginningless in time.

children.text: yas tv asāv ekabhavikaḥ karmāśayaḥ sa niyatavipākaścāniyatavipākaśca ||
children.translated_text: But that one-birth-producing <s>karmāśaya</s> is both of fixed fruition and of unfixed fruition.

children.text: tatra dṛṣṭajanmavedanīyasya niyatavipākasyaivāyaṃ niyamo na tv adṛṣṭajanmavedanīyasyāniyatavipākasya ||
children.translated_text: Here this rule applies only to what is to be experienced in the visible birth and has fixed fruition, not to what is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has unfixed fruition.
Why?
For what is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has unfixed fruition has a threefold course.

children.text: kṛtasyāvipakvasya vināśaḥ pradhānakarmaṇy āvāpagamanaṃ vā niyatavipākapradhānakarmaṇābhibhūtasya vā ciram avasthānam iti ||
children.translated_text: There is the destruction of what has been done but has not ripened, or its entry as an admixture into a principal action, or its long persistence when overpowered by a principal action of fixed fruition.

children.text: tatra kṛtasyāvipakvasya nāśo yathā śuklakarmodayād ihaiva nāśaḥ kṛṣṇasya ||
children.translated_text: Among these, the destruction of what has been done but has not ripened is like the destruction, in this very life, of black action through the rise of white action.
On this point it has been said:

children.text: dve dve ha vai karmaṇī veditavye pāpakasyaiko rāśiḥ puṇyakṛto 'pahanti ||
children.translated_text: Two and two kinds of action are to be known: one heap belonging to the evil-doer is destroyed by the maker of merit.

children.text: tad icchasva karmāṇi sukṛtāni kartum ihaiva te karma kavayo vedayante ||
children.translated_text: Therefore desire to perform well-done actions; here itself the wise make your action known to you.
Its entry as an admixture into a principal action:
On this point it has been said:

children.text: syāt svalpaḥ saṃkaraḥ saparihāraḥ sapratyavamarṣaḥ kuśalasya nāpakarṣāyālam ||
children.translated_text: There may be a small admixture, accompanied by a remedy and by reflective correction; it is not sufficient to draw down the wholesome.
Why?

children.text: kuśalaṃ hi me bahvanyad asti yatrāyam āvāpaṃ gataḥ svarge 'py apakarṣam alpaṃ kariṣyatīti ||
children.translated_text: For one thinks, 'I have much other wholesome karma, into which this has entered as an admixture; even in heaven it will cause only a slight diminution.'
