Or there is the long persistence of what has been overpowered by a principal action of fixed fruition.
How so?
This rule applies to what is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has fixed fruition, but not to what is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has unfixed fruition.

children.text: yat tvadṛṣṭajanmavedanīyaṃ karmāniyatavipākaṃ tan naśyed āvāpaṃ vā gacched abhibhūtaṃ vā ciram apyupāsīta yāvat samānaṃ karmābhivyañjakaṃ nimittam asya na vipākābhimukhaṃ karotīti ||
children.translated_text: But action that is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has unfixed fruition may perish, or enter as an admixture, or, being overpowered, may remain for a long time, until a similar action, serving as its manifesting cause, turns it toward fruition.

children.text: tadvipākasyaiva deśakālanimittānavadhāraṇād iyaṃ karmagatir vicitrā durvijñānā ceti ||
children.translated_text: Because the place, time, and occasion of that fruition are not fixed, this course of karma is varied and difficult to understand.

children.text: na cotsargasyāpavādān nivṛttir ityekabhavikaḥ karmāśayo 'nujñāyata iti ||
children.translated_text: And an exception does not annul the general rule; thus the one-birth-producing <s>karmāśaya</s> is accepted.

children.text: te janmāyurbhogāḥ puṇyahetukāḥ sukhaphalā apuṇyahetukā duḥkhaphalā iti ||
children.translated_text: Those births, lifespans, and experiences, when caused by merit, have pleasure as their fruit; when caused by demerit, they have pain as their fruit.

children.text: yathā cedaṃ duḥkhaṃ pratikūlātmakam evaṃ viṣayasukhakāle 'pi duḥkham asty eva pratikūlātmakaṃ yoginaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And just as this pain is by nature adverse, so even at the time of pleasure in objects there is indeed pain, adverse by nature, for the yogin.
How is that established?

children.text: sarvasyāyaṃ rāgānuviddhaś cetanācetanasādhanādhīnaḥ sukhānubhava iti tatrāsti rāgajaḥ karmāśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For everyone, the experience of pleasure is pervaded by <s>rāga</s> and depends on conscious and unconscious means; therefore there is in it a <s>karmāśaya</s> born of rāga.

children.text: tathā ca dveṣṭi duḥkhasādhanāni muhyati ceti ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, one hates the means of pain and becomes deluded.
There is also a <s>karmāśaya</s> produced by hatred and delusion.
And so it has been said:
Enjoyment is not possible without injuring living beings.
There is also bodily karma produced by violence.
And object-pleasure has been called <s>avidyā</s>.

children.text: yā bhogeṣv indriyāṇāṃ tṛpter upaśāntis tat sukham ||
children.translated_text: The quieting of the satisfaction of the senses in enjoyments is pleasure.
The non-quieting caused by restlessness is pain.

children.text: na cendriyāṇāṃ bhogābhyāsena vaitṛṣṇyaṃ kartuṃ śakyam ||
children.translated_text: And dispassion in the senses cannot be produced by repeated enjoyment.
Why?

children.text: yato bhogābhyāsam anu vivardhante rāgāḥ kauśalāni cendriyāṇām iti ||
children.translated_text: Because, following upon repeated enjoyment, passions and the capacities of the senses increase.
Therefore repeated enjoyment is not a means to pleasure.

children.text: sa khalv ayaṃ vṛścikaviṣabhīta ivāśīviṣeṇa daṣṭo yaḥ sukhārthī ||
children.translated_text: Indeed, the person who seeks pleasure is like one afraid of scorpion poison who has been bitten by a venomous snake.
Imbued with objects, he is sunk in a great mire of suffering.

children.text: eṣā pariṇāmaduḥkhatā nāma pratikūlā sukhāvasthāyām api yoginam eva kliśnāti ||
children.translated_text: This is called the painfulness of transformation; it is adverse, and it afflicts the yogin alone even in a state of pleasure.
Now, what is the painfulness of anxiety?

children.text: sarvasya dveṣānuviddhaś cetanācetanasādhanādhīnas tāpānubhava iti tatrāsti dveṣajaḥ karmāśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For everyone, the experience of anxiety is pervaded by hatred and depends on conscious and unconscious means; therefore there is in it a <s>karmāśaya</s> born of hatred.

children.text: sukhasādhanāni ca prārthayamānaḥ kāyena vācā manasā ca parispandate tataḥ param anugṛhṇāty upahanti ceti ||
children.translated_text: And while he seeks the means of pleasure, he moves with body, speech, and mind; thereafter he either favors another or harms him.
Through benefiting and injuring others he accumulates <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>.

children.text: sa karmāśayo lobhān mohācca bhavatīty eṣā tāpaduḥkhatocyate ||
children.translated_text: That karmic deposit arises from greed and from delusion; this is called the painfulness of anxiety.
What, then, is the painfulness of latent impressions?

children.text: sukhānubhavāt sukhasaṃskārāśayo duḥkhānubhavād api duḥkhasaṃskārāśaya iti ||
children.translated_text: From the experience of pleasure there is a deposit of latent impressions of pleasure, and from the experience of pain there is also a deposit of latent impressions of pain.

children.text: evaṃ karmabhyo vipāke 'nubhūyamāne sukhe duḥkhe vā punaḥ karmāśayapracaya iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, while pleasure or pain is being experienced as the fruition of actions, there is again an accumulation of karmic deposit.

children.text: evam idam anādi duḥkhasroto viprasṛtaṃ yoginam eva pratikūlātmakatvād udvejayati ||
children.translated_text: In this way this beginningless stream of suffering, spread abroad, disturbs only the yogin, because its nature is adverse to him.
Why?
For the learned person is like the vessel of the eye.

children.text: yathorṇātantur akṣipātre nyastaḥ sparśena duḥkhayati nānyeṣu gātrāvayaveṣu evam etāni duḥkhāny akṣipātrakalpaṃ yoginam eva kliśnanti netaraṃ pratipattāram ||
children.translated_text: Just as a woolen thread placed in the eye-bowl causes pain by its touch, but not on other limbs of the body, so these sufferings afflict only the yogin, who is like the eye-bowl, and not another knower.

children.text: itaraṃ tu svakarmopahṛtaṃ duḥkham upāttam upāttaṃ tyajantaṃ tyaktaṃ tyaktam upādadānam anādivāsanāvicitrayā cittavṛttyā samantato 'nuviddham ivāvidyāyā hātavya evāhaṃkāramamakārānupātinaṃ jātaṃ jātaṃ bāhyādhyātmikobhayanimittās triparvāṇas tāpā anuplavante ||
children.translated_text: But another person, pierced on every side, as it were, by a mental activity variegated with beginningless latent impressions, takes up pain brought on by his own action and then abandons what has been taken up, and takes up again what has been abandoned; born again and again, he is pursued by the threefold torments, arising from external, internal, and both kinds of causes, following upon <s>avidyā</s> and upon the notions of 'I' and 'mine,' and surely to be abandoned.

children.text: tad evam anādinā duḥkhasrotasā vyuhyamānam ātmānaṃ bhūtagrāmaṃ ca dṛṣṭvā yogī sarvaduḥkhakṣayakāraṇaṃ samyagdarśanaṃ śaraṇaṃ prapadyata iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, seeing himself and the mass of beings being carried along by the beginningless stream of suffering, the yogin resorts to right vision as the cause of the destruction of all suffering.

children.text: guṇavṛttivirodhāc ca duḥkham eva sarvaṃ vivekinaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And because of the opposition among the activities of the guṇas, for the discriminating one everything is nothing but pain.

children.text: prakhyāpravṛttisthitirūpā buddhiguṇāḥ parasparānugrahatantrībhūtvā śāntaṃ ghoraṃ mūḍhaṃ vā pratyayaṃ triguṇam evārabhante ||
children.translated_text: The qualities of the intellect, whose forms are illumination, activity, and steadiness, being dependent on mutual support, produce a cognition that is calm, terrible, or dull, and is itself constituted by the three guṇas.

children.text: calaṃ ca guṇavṛttam iti kṣiprapariṇāmi cittam uktam ||
children.translated_text: And the activity of the guṇas is mobile; thus the mind has been said to transform quickly.

children.text: rūpātiśayā vṛttyatiśayāśca paraspareṇa virudhyante sāmānyāni tv atiśayaiḥ saha pravartante ||
children.translated_text: Special forms and special activities conflict with one another, while common features proceed together with the special features.

children.text: evam ete guṇā itaretarāśrayeṇopārjitasukhaduḥkhamohapratyayāḥ sarve sarvarūpā bhavantīti guṇapradhānabhāvakṛtas tv eṣāṃ viśeṣa iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus these guṇas, by their mutual dependence, acquire cognitions of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and all become of every form; but their distinction is produced by the predominance or subordination of the guṇas.

children.text: tasmād duḥkham eva sarvaṃ vivekina iti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, for the discriminating one everything is nothing but pain.

children.text: tad asya mahato duḥkhasamudāyasya prabhavabījam avidyā ||
children.translated_text: Accordingly, the seed from which this great mass of suffering arises is <s>avidyā</s>.
And right vision is the cause of its absence.

children.text: yathā cikitsāśāstraṃ caturvyūhaṃ rogo rogahetur ārogyaṃ bhaiṣajyam iti evam idam api śāstraṃ caturvyūham eva ||
children.translated_text: Just as medical science has a fourfold arrangement: disease, the cause of disease, health, and medicine; so too this śāstra has exactly a fourfold arrangement.

children.text: tad yathā saṃsāraḥ saṃsārahetur mokṣo mokṣopāya iti ||
children.translated_text: That is: <s>saṃsāra</s>, the cause of <s>saṃsāra</s>, liberation, and the means to liberation.
There, <s>saṃsāra</s>, being full of suffering, is what is to be abandoned.
The conjunction of <s>pradhāna</s> and <s>puruṣa</s> is the cause of what is to be abandoned.
The absolute cessation of that conjunction is abandonment.
Right vision is the means of abandonment.

children.text: tatra hātuḥ svarūpam upādeyaṃ vā heyaṃ vā na bhavitum arhati ||
children.translated_text: In this matter, the own nature of the abandoner cannot properly be either something to be appropriated or something to be abandoned.

children.text: hāne tasyocchedavādaprasaṅgaḥ upādāne ca hetuvādaḥ ubhayapratyākhyāne ca śāśvatavāda ity etat samyagdarśanam ||
children.translated_text: If it were abandoned, the doctrine of annihilation would follow; if it were appropriated, there would be a doctrine of causation; and if both were rejected, there would be a doctrine of eternality. This is right vision.
This śāstra, then, is said to have a fourfold arrangement.

children.text: duḥkham atītam upabhogenātivāhitaṃ na heyapakṣe vartate ||
children.translated_text: Past suffering, having been passed beyond through experience, does not fall on the side of what is to be abandoned.

children.text: vartamānaṃ ca svakṣaṇe bhogārūḍham iti na tatkṣaṇāntare heyatām āpadyate ||
children.translated_text: And present suffering, having already mounted into experience in its own moment, does not become something to be abandoned in another moment.

children.text: tasmād yad evānāgataṃ duḥkhaṃ tad evākṣipātrakalpaṃ yoginaṃ kliśnāti netaraṃ pratipattāram ||
children.translated_text: Therefore only future suffering is what afflicts the yogin, who is like the eye-bowl, and not another knower.
That alone becomes something to be abandoned.

children.text: tasmād yad eva heyam ity ucyate tasyaiva kāraṇaṃ pratinirdiśyate ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, only of that which is called 'to be abandoned' is the cause specifically indicated.
The seer is <s>puruṣa</s>, the one who is aware of the intellect.
The seen consists of all dharmas mounted upon the sattva of the intellect.

children.text: tad etad dṛśyam ayaskāntamaṇikalpaṃ saṃnidhimātropakāri dṛśyatvena svaṃ bhavati puruṣasya dṛśirūpasya svāminaḥ ||
children.translated_text: This seen, like a lodestone, assists by mere proximity; as an object of sight it becomes the property of <s>puruṣa</s>, its master, whose nature is seeing.

children.text: anubhavakarmaviṣayatām āpannam tayor dṛgdarśanaśaktyor anādir arthakṛtaḥ saṃyogo heyahetur duḥkhasya kāraṇam ity arthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: It has become the object of the action of experience. The beginningless conjunction of those two powers, seeing and vision, brought about for the sake of purpose, is the cause of what is to be abandoned, that is, the cause of suffering.
And so it has been said:
By avoiding the cause of that conjunction, there would be this absolute remedy for suffering.
Why?
Because a remedy is seen for the avoidable cause of suffering.

children.text: tad yathā pādatalasya bhedyatā kaṇṭakasya bhettṛtvaṃ parihāraḥ kaṇṭakasya pādānadhiṣṭhānaṃ pādatrāṇavyavahitena vādhiṣṭhānam ||
children.translated_text: For example, there is the penetrability of the sole of the foot, the piercing power of a thorn, and avoidance: the thorn's not being placed under the foot, or its being placed there with the intervention of footwear.

children.text: etat trayaṃ yo veda loke sa tatra pratīkāram ārabhamāṇo bhedajaṃ duḥkhaṃ nāpnoti ||
children.translated_text: Whoever knows these three in the world, when undertaking the remedy in that case, does not incur the pain produced by piercing.
Why?
Because of the power of apprehending the triad.

children.text: atrāpi tāpakasya rajasaḥ sattvam eva tapyaṃ ||
children.translated_text: Here too, of <s>rajas</s>, which burns, <s>sattva</s> alone is what is burned.
Why?
Because the action of burning rests in an object.

children.text: sattve karmaṇi tapikriyā nāpariṇāmini niṣkriye kṣetrajñe ||
children.translated_text: The action of burning occurs in <s>sattva</s> as the object of action, not in the unchanging and inactive knower of the field.

children.text: darśitaviṣayatvāt sattve tu tapyamāne tadākārānurodhī puruṣo 'nutapyata iti dṛśyasvarūpam ucyate ||
children.translated_text: Because the object has been shown: when <s>sattva</s> is being burned, <s>puruṣa</s>, conforming to that form, is as though burned along with it. Thus the nature of the seen is being stated.
<s>Sattva</s> has the nature of illumination.
<s>Rajas</s> has the nature of activity.
<s>tamas</s> is characterized by stability.

children.text: ete guṇāḥ parasparoparaktapravibhāgāḥ pariṇāminaḥ saṃyogavibhāgadharmāṇa itaretaropāśrayeṇopārjitamūrtayaḥ parasparāṅgāṅgitve 'pyasaṃbhinnaśaktipravibhāgās tulyajātīyātulyajātīyaśaktibhedānupātinaḥ pradhānavelāyām upadarśitasaṃnidhānā guṇatve 'pi ca vyāpāramātreṇa pradhānāntarṇītānumitāstitāḥ puruṣārthakartavyatayā prayuktasāmarthyāḥ saṃnidhimātropakāriṇo 'yaskāntamaṇikalpāḥ pratyayam antareṇaikatamasya vṛttim anuvartamānāḥ pradhānaśabdavācyā bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: These guṇas, mutually colored by one another and yet divided, subject to transformation, possessing the properties of conjunction and separation, acquiring their forms through mutual dependence, though standing as limb and principal for one another, nevertheless have distinct divisions of power that are not confused. They follow differences of powers both of the same class and of different classes; at the boundary-state of pradhāna they display proximity; though they are guṇas, their existence is inferred as included within pradhāna merely by their activity. Their capacity is set in motion for the sake of the purpose of <s>puruṣa</s>; they assist by mere proximity, like a lodestone; without any cognition, following the activity of any one among them, they come to be denoted by the word <s>pradhāna</s>.
This is called the seen object.

children.text: tad etad bhūtendriyātmakaṃ bhūtabhāvena pṛthivyādinā sūkṣmasthūlena pariṇamate tathendriyabhāvena śrotrādinā sūkṣmasthūlena pariṇamata iti ||
children.translated_text: This, consisting of elements and senses, transforms, in the condition of elements, as earth and the others, subtle and gross; and likewise it transforms, in the condition of senses, as hearing and the others, subtle and gross.

children.text: tat tu nāprayojanam api tu prayojanam urarīkṛtya pravartata iti bhogāpavargārthaṃ hi tad dṛśyaṃ puruṣasyeti ||
children.translated_text: But it does not proceed without a purpose; rather, it proceeds after accepting a purpose. For that seen object is for the sake of experience and liberation for <s>puruṣa</s>.

children.text: tatreṣṭāniṣṭaguṇasvarūpāvadhāraṇam avibhāgāpannaṃ bhogaḥ bhoktuḥ svarūpāvadhāraṇam apavarga iti ||
children.translated_text: There, the ascertainment of the nature of desirable and undesirable qualities, when it has fallen into non-distinction, is experience. The ascertainment of the experiencer's own nature is liberation.
There is no other seeing beyond these two.
And so it has been said:

children.text: ayaṃ tu khalu triṣu guṇeṣu kartṛṣv akartari ca puruṣe tulyātulyajātīye caturthe tatkriyāsākṣiṇy upanīyamānān sarvabhāvān upapannān anupaśyan na darśanam anyacchaṅkate iti ||
children.translated_text: Seeing all entities brought before the three guṇas, which are agents, and before <s>puruṣa</s>, which is a non-agent, a fourth thing, of a similar and dissimilar class, and the witness of their activity, he regards them all as fitting and does not suspect any other seeing.

children.text: tāv etau bhogāpavargau buddhikṛtau buddhāv eva vartamānau kathaṃ puruṣe vyapadiśyete iti ||
children.translated_text: These two, experience and liberation, are produced by the intellect and exist only in the intellect; how then are they predicated of <s>puruṣa</s>?

children.text: yathā ca jayaḥ parājayo vā yoddhṛṣu vartamānaḥ svāmini vyapadiśyate sa hi tatphalasya bhokteti evaṃ bandhamokṣau buddhāv eva vartamānau puruṣe vyapadiśyete sa hi tatphalasya bhokteti ||
children.translated_text: Just as victory or defeat, though existing among the warriors, is predicated of the master, for he is the experiencer of its result, so bondage and liberation, though existing only in the intellect, are predicated of <s>puruṣa</s>, for he is the experiencer of their result.

children.text: buddher eva puruṣārthāparisamāptir bandhas tadarthāvasāyo mokṣa iti ||
children.translated_text: The intellect's non-completion of the purpose of <s>puruṣa</s> is bondage; the cessation of its purpose for him is liberation.

children.text: etena grahaṇadhāraṇohāpohatattvajñānābhiniveśā buddhau vartamānāḥ puruṣe 'dhyāropitasadbhāvāḥ sa hi tatphalasya bhokteti ||
children.translated_text: By this, grasping, retention, reasoning, rejection, knowledge of reality, and attachment, which exist in the intellect, are explained as having their existence superimposed on <s>puruṣa</s>, for he is the experiencer of their result.

children.text: dṛśyānāṃ tu guṇānāṃ svarūpabhedāvadhāraṇārtham idam ārabhyate ||
children.translated_text: Now this is begun in order to determine the distinctions in nature among the guṇas that are the seen objects.
There, space, wind, fire, water, and earth are the elements, the specific forms of the non-specific sound-tanmātra, touch-tanmātra, form-tanmātra, taste-tanmātra, and smell-tanmātra.

children.text: tathā śrotratvakcakṣurjihvāghrāṇāni buddhīndriyāṇi vākyapāṇipādapāyūpasthāni karmendriyāṇi ekādaśaṃ manaḥ sarvārtham ity etāny asmitālakṣaṇasyāviśeṣasya viśeṣāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Likewise hearing, skin, sight, tongue, and smell are the cognitive senses; speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals are the active senses; the eleventh is mind, whose object is everything. These are the specific forms of the non-specific entity characterized by asmitā.
This set of sixteen is the specific transformation of the guṇas.
There are six non-specifics.
That is as follows:

children.text: śabdatanmātraṃ sparśatanmātraṃ rūpatanmātraṃ rasatanmātraṃ gandhatanmātraṃ cety ekadvitricatuṣpañcalakṣaṇāḥ śabdādayaḥ pañcāviśeṣāḥ ṣaṣṭhaścāviśeṣo 'smitāmātra iti ||
children.translated_text: The sound-tanmātra, touch-tanmātra, form-tanmātra, taste-tanmātra, and smell-tanmātra: sound and the rest, characterized by one, two, three, four, and five properties, are the five non-specifics; and the sixth non-specific is mere asmitā.
These are the six non-specific transformations of the great self, whose nature is mere being.

children.text: yat tatparam aviśeṣebhyo liṅgamātraṃ mahattattvaṃ tasminn ete sattāmātre mahaty ātmany avasthāya vivṛddhikāṣṭhām anubhavanti pratisaṃsṛjyamānāśca tasminn eva sattāmātre mahaty ātmany avasthāya yat tan niḥsattāsattaṃ niḥsadasan nirasad avyaktam aliṅgaṃ pradhānaṃ tat pratiyanti ||
children.translated_text: That which is higher than the non-specifics is the mere mark, the principle of mahat. Having rested in that great self of mere being, these undergo the highest development; and when they are being reabsorbed, having rested in that same great self of mere being, they go back to that which is neither existent nor non-existent, neither real nor unreal, not unreal, unmanifest, without mark, namely pradhāna.

children.text: eṣa teṣāṃ liṅgamātraḥ pariṇāmo niḥsattāsattaṃ cāliṅgapariṇāma iti ||
children.translated_text: This is their transformation as the mere mark, and that which is neither existent nor non-existent is the transformation without mark.
In the state without mark, the purpose of <s>puruṣa</s> is not the cause.

children.text: nāliṅgāvasthāyām ādau puruṣārthatā kāraṇaṃ bhavatīti na tasyāḥ puruṣārthatā kāraṇaṃ bhavatīti nāsau puruṣārthakṛteti nityākhyāyate ||
children.translated_text: At the beginning, in the state without mark, being for the sake of <s>puruṣa</s> is not the cause; therefore being for the sake of <s>puruṣa</s> is not the cause of it; therefore it is not produced for the sake of <s>puruṣa</s>, and so it is called eternal.

children.text: trayāṇāṃ tv avasthāviśeṣāṇām ādau puruṣārthatā kāraṇaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: But at the beginning of the three special states, being for the sake of <s>puruṣa</s> is the cause.

children.text: sa cārtho hetur nimittaṃ kāraṇaṃ bhavatīty anityākhyāyate ||
children.translated_text: And that purpose becomes the motive, occasion, and cause; therefore they are called non-eternal.

children.text: guṇās tu sarvadharmānupātino na pratyastam ayante nopajāyante ||
children.translated_text: But the guṇas, which accompany all properties, neither cease nor arise.

children.text: vyaktibhir evātītānāgatavyayāgamavatībhir guṇānvayinībhir upajananāpāyadharmakā iva pratyavabhāsante ||
children.translated_text: They merely appear as if they had the property of origination and disappearance through manifestations that have passing away and coming into being in the past and future, while those manifestations are accompanied by the guṇas.
For example, '<s>Devadatta</s> becomes poor.'
Why?
Because his cows die.

children.text: gavām eva maraṇāt tasya daridratā na svarūpahānād iti samaḥ samādhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because only the cows die, his poverty is not due to loss of his own nature. The same conclusion applies here.

children.text: liṅgamātram aliṅgasya pratyāsannaṃ tatra tatsaṃsṛṣṭaṃ vivicyate kramānativṛtteḥ ||
children.translated_text: The mere mark is proximate to the markless; there, what is mingled with it is separated out, because the sequence is not overstepped.

children.text: tathā ṣaḍ aviśeṣā liṅgamātre saṃsṛṣṭā vivicyante pariṇāmakramaniyamāt ||
children.translated_text: Likewise the six non-specifics, mingled in the mere mark, are separated out because of the fixed order of transformation.

children.text: tathā teṣv aviśeṣeṣu bhūtendriyāṇi saṃsṛṣṭāni vivicyante tathā coktaṃ purastāt ||
children.translated_text: Likewise the elements and senses, mingled in those non-specifics, are separated out; and so it was said earlier.

children.text: na viśeṣebhyaḥ paraṃ tattvāntaram astīti viśeṣāṇāṃ nāsti tattvāntarapariṇāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: There is no further principle beyond the specifics; therefore the specifics have no transformation into another principle.
But their transformations of property, characteristic, and state will be explained.
The seen object has been explained.
Now this is begun in order to determine the own nature of the seer.

children.text: dṛśimātra iti dṛkśaktir eva viśeṣaṇāparāmṛṣṭety arthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "Only seeing" means that it is the power of seeing alone, untouched by any qualification.
That <s>puruṣa</s> is the witness-consciousness of the intellect.

children.text: sa buddher na sarūpo nātyantaṃ virūpa iti ||
children.translated_text: He is neither of the same form as the intellect nor utterly different in form from it.
First, he is not of the same form.
Why?

children.text: jñātājñātaviṣayatvāt pariṇāminī hi buddhiḥ tasyāśca viṣayo gavādir ghaṭādir vā jñātaścājñātaśceti pariṇāmitvaṃ darśayati ||
children.translated_text: Because the intellect has objects that are known and unknown. For the intellect is subject to transformation, and its object, whether a cow and the like or a pot and the like, is sometimes known and sometimes unknown; thus it shows its transformability.
But the fact that the object is always known for <s>puruṣa</s> makes clear his non-transformability.
Why?

children.text: na hi buddhiśca nāma puruṣaviṣayaśca syād gṛhītāgṛhītā ceti siddhaṃ puruṣasya sadājñātaviṣayatvaṃ tataścāpariṇāmitvam iti ||
children.translated_text: For the intellect could not be both intellect and an object of <s>puruṣa</s>, both apprehended and not apprehended. Thus it is established that the object is always known for <s>puruṣa</s>, and from that his non-transformability.

children.text: kiṃ ca parārthā buddhiḥ saṃhatyakāritvāt svārthaḥ puruṣa iti ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, the intellect exists for another's sake, because it acts through aggregation; <s>puruṣa</s> exists for his own sake.

children.text: tathā sarvārthādhyavasāyakatvāt triguṇā buddhis triguṇatvād acetaneti ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, because the intellect determines all objects, it consists of the three <s>guṇa</s>s; because it consists of the three <s>guṇa</s>s, it is unconscious.
But <s>puruṣa</s> is the overseer of the <s>guṇa</s>s.
Therefore he is not of the same form.
Then let him be different in form.
He is not utterly different in form.
Why?
Though pure, he is one who observes the mental presentations.
For he observes the presentation belonging to the intellect.

children.text: tam anupaśyann atadātmāpi tadātmaka iva pratyavabhāsate ||
children.translated_text: Observing it, though not identical with it, he appears as if he had its nature.
And so it has been said:

children.text: apariṇāminī hi bhoktṛśaktir apratisaṃkramā ca pariṇāminyarthe pratisaṃkrānteva tadvṛttim anupatati tasyāśca prāptacaitanyopagraharūpāyā buddhivṛtter anukāramātratayā buddhivṛttyaviśiṣṭā hi jñānavṛttir ity ākhyāyate ||
children.translated_text: For the power of experiencing is unchanging and does not pass over; yet with regard to a changing object it appears to pass over and follows that object's mode. Since the mode of intellect has obtained the support of consciousness, the mode of knowledge is spoken of as not distinct from the mode of intellect, because it is merely an imitation of that mode.

children.text: dṛśirūpasya puruṣasya karmarūpatām āpannaṃ dṛśyam iti tadartha eva dṛśyasyātmā svarūpaṃ bhavatīty arthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The seen, having come to be an object-form for <s>puruṣa</s>, whose nature is seeing, has its own being and own nature only for his sake. This is the meaning.

children.text: tatsvarūpaṃ tu pararūpeṇa pratilabdhātmakaṃ bhogāpavargārthatāyāṃ kṛtāyāṃ puruṣeṇa na dṛśyata iti ||
children.translated_text: But when its own nature, having gained its identity through the form of another, has accomplished the purposes of experience and liberation, it is no longer seen by <s>puruṣa</s>.

children.text: svarūpahānād asya nāśaḥ prāptaḥ na tu vinaśyati ||
children.translated_text: Because its own form is lost, its destruction follows; yet it does not perish.
Why?

children.text: kṛtārtham ekaṃ puruṣaṃ prati dṛśyaṃ naṣṭam api nāśaṃ prāptam apy anaṣṭaṃ tad anyapuruṣasādhāraṇatvāt ||
children.translated_text: The seen, though destroyed with respect to one <s>puruṣa</s> whose purpose has been fulfilled, and though it has reached destruction, is still not destroyed, because it is common to other <s>puruṣa</s>s.

children.text: kuśalaṃ puruṣaṃ prati nāśaṃ prāptam apy akuśalān puruṣān prati na kṛtārtham iti teṣāṃ dṛśeḥ karmaviṣayatām āpannaṃ labhate eva pararūpeṇātmarūpam iti ||
children.translated_text: Though it has reached destruction with respect to a skilled <s>puruṣa</s>, it has not fulfilled its purpose with respect to unskilled <s>puruṣa</s>s; therefore, having become an object of action for their seeing, it indeed obtains its own form through the form of another.

children.text: ataśca dṛgdarśanaśaktyor nityatvād anādiḥ saṃyogo vyākhyāta iti ||
children.translated_text: And therefore, since the powers of seeing and of the seen are eternal, their conjunction has been explained as beginningless.
And so it has been said:

children.text: dharmiṇām anādisaṃyogād dharmamātrāṇām apy anādiḥ saṃyoga iti ||
children.translated_text: Because the substrates have beginningless conjunction, the mere properties too have beginningless conjunction.
This sūtra was set forth with the intention of stating the nature of conjunction.

children.text: puruṣaḥ svāmī dṛśyena svena darśanārthaṃ saṃyuktaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Puruṣa</s>, the master, is conjoined with his own seen object for the sake of seeing.

children.text: tasmāt saṃyogād dṛśyasyopalabdhir yā sa bhogaḥ yā tu draṣṭuḥ svarūpopalabdhiḥ so 'pavargaḥ ||
children.translated_text: From that conjunction, the apprehension of the seen is experience; but the apprehension of the seer's own nature is liberation.

children.text: darśanakāryāvasānaḥ saṃyoga iti darśanaṃ viyogasya kāraṇam uktam ||
children.translated_text: Conjunction ends when the work of seeing is complete; thus seeing has been stated as the cause of separation.

children.text: darśanam adarśanasya pratidvaṃdvīty adarśanaṃ saṃyoganimittam uktam ||
children.translated_text: Since seeing is opposed to non-seeing, non-seeing has been stated as the cause of conjunction.

children.text: nātra darśanaṃ mokṣakāraṇam adarśanābhāvād eva bandhābhāvaḥ sa mokṣa iti ||
children.translated_text: Here seeing is not the cause of liberation; rather, because of the absence of non-seeing there is absence of bondage, and that is liberation.

children.text: darśanasya bhāve bandhakāraṇasyādarśanasya nāśa ity ato darśanajñānaṃ kaivalyakāraṇam uktam ||
children.translated_text: When seeing is present, the non-seeing that is the cause of bondage is destroyed; therefore the knowledge that is seeing is said to be the cause of <s>kaivalya</s>.
And what is this thing called non-seeing?
Is it the active authority of the <s>guṇa</s>s?

children.text: āhosvid dṛśirūpasya svāmino darśitaviṣayasya pradhānacittasyānutpādaḥ svasmin dṛśye vidyamāne darśanābhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Or is it the non-arising of the primary mind for the master whose nature is seeing and to whom an object has been shown, that is, the absence of seeing while its own seen object is present?
Is it the meaningfulness of the <s>guṇa</s>s?
Or is it ignorance, restrained together with its own mind, as the seed for the arising of its own mind?
Is it, when the impressions of stability have been exhausted, the manifestation of the impressions of motion?
In this connection the following has been said:

children.text: pradhānaṃ sthityaiva vartamānaṃ vikārākaraṇād apradhānaṃ syāt tathā gatyaiva vartamānaṃ vikāranityatvād apradhānaṃ syāt ||
children.translated_text: <s>Pradhāna</s>, if it were functioning only by stability, would be non-primary because it would not produce modifications; likewise, if it were functioning only by motion, it would be non-primary because modifications would be eternal.

children.text: ubhayathā cāsya pravṛttiḥ pradhānavyavahāraṃ labhate nānyathā ||
children.translated_text: Only when its activity is in both ways does it receive the conventional designation <s>pradhāna</s>; not otherwise.
Even if other causes are imagined, the same discussion applies.
Some say that the power of seeing itself is non-seeing.
For scripture says that the activity of <s>pradhāna</s> is for the purpose of revealing itself.

children.text: sarvabodhyabodhasamarthaḥ prākpravṛtteḥ puruṣo na paśyati sarvakāryakaraṇasamarthaṃ dṛśyaṃ tadā na dṛśyata iti ||
children.translated_text: Before activity begins, <s>puruṣa</s>, though capable of cognizing all that can be cognized, does not see; and the seen, though capable of all effects and instruments, is not then seen.
Some say that non-seeing is a property of both.

children.text: tatredaṃ dṛśyasya svātmabhūtam api puruṣapratyayāpekṣaṃ darśanaṃ dṛśyadharmatvena bhavati tathā puruṣasyānātmabhūtam api dṛśyapratyayāpekṣaṃ puruṣadharmatveneva darśanam avabhāsate ||
children.translated_text: In this matter, seeing, though belonging to the own nature of the seen, depends on a presentation to <s>puruṣa</s> and so exists as a property of the seen; likewise, seeing, though not belonging to the own nature of <s>puruṣa</s>, depends on a presentation of the seen and appears as if it were a property of <s>puruṣa</s>.
Some say that the knowledge which is seeing itself is non-seeing.
These are the alternatives found in the treatise.

children.text: tatra vikalpabahutvam etat sarvapuruṣāṇām guṇānāṃ saṃyoge sādhāraṇaviṣayam ||
children.translated_text: Among them, this multiplicity of alternatives has as its common object the conjunction of the <s>guṇa</s>s with all <s>puruṣa</s>s.
But the conjunction of the inward consciousness with its own intellect
means the latent impression of erroneous knowledge.

children.text: viparyayajñānavāsanāvāsitā ca na kāryaniṣṭhāṃ puruṣakhyātiṃ buddhiḥ prāpnoti sādhikārā punar āvartate ||
children.translated_text: And the intellect, perfumed by the latent impressions of erroneous knowledge, does not attain the completion of its task, namely knowledge of <s>puruṣa</s>; while its authority remains, it turns back again.

children.text: sā tu puruṣakhyātiparyavasānā kāryaniṣṭhāṃ prāpnoti caritādhikārā nivṛttādarśanā bandhakāraṇābhāvān na punar āvartate ||
children.translated_text: But when it ends in knowledge of <s>puruṣa</s>, it attains the completion of its task; its authority has been fulfilled, seeing has ceased, and because the cause of bondage is absent, it does not turn back again.
Here someone raises an objection by means of the story of the eunuch.
A eunuch is addressed by his foolish wife:

children.text: āryaputra apatyavatī me bhaginī kimarthaṃ nāham iti ||
children.translated_text: “Noble husband, my sister has children; why do I not?”
He says to her:
“When I am dead, I shall beget a child for you.”

children.text: tathedaṃ vidyamānaṃ jñānaṃ cittanivṛttiṃ na karoti vinaṣṭaṃ kariṣyatīti kā pratyāśā ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, if this knowledge, while present, does not bring about the cessation of the mind, what hope is there that it will do so when it has perished?
On this point one who has the standing of a teacher says:

children.text: nanu buddhinivṛttir eva mokṣaḥ adarśanakāraṇābhāvād buddhinivṛttiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Surely liberation is just the cessation of the intellect; because the cause of non-seeing is absent, the intellect ceases.
And that non-seeing, the cause of bondage, ceases through seeing.
Therefore cessation of the mind itself is liberation.
Why, then, is his confusion of thought directed at an inappropriate point?
The pain to be removed has been stated.
And the cause of what is to be removed, called conjunction and together with its occasion, has been stated.
After this, removal must be stated.

children.text: tasyādarśanasyābhāvād buddhipuruṣasaṃyogābhāva ātyantiko bandhanoparama ity arthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because that non-seeing is absent, the conjunction of intellect and <s>puruṣa</s> is absolutely absent; this means the cessation of bondage.
This is removal.

children.text: tad dṛśeḥ kaivalyaṃ puruṣasyāmiśrībhāvaḥ punar asaṃyogo guṇair ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: That is the isolation of the power of seeing, <s>kaivalya</s> for <s>puruṣa</s>: the state of being unmixed, that is, renewed non-conjunction with the guṇas.

children.text: duḥkhakāraṇanivṛttau duḥkhoparamo hānaṃ tadā svarūpapratiṣṭhaḥ puruṣa ityuktam ||
children.translated_text: When the cause of pain has ceased, the cessation of pain is removal; then <s>puruṣa</s> is established in its own nature, as has been stated.
Now, what is the means for attaining that removal?
The cognition of the difference between <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s> is discriminative knowledge.
But when false knowledge has not ceased, it wavers.

children.text: yadā mithyājñānaṃ dagdhabījabhāvaṃ bandhyaprasavaṃ sampadyate tadā vidhūtakleśarajasaḥ sattvasya pare vaiśāradye parasyāṃ vaśīkārasaṃjñāyāṃ vartamānasya vivekapratyayapravāho nirmalo bhavati ||
children.translated_text: When false knowledge becomes like a burnt seed, incapable of producing offspring, then, in the supreme clarity of <s>sattva</s>, whose dust of afflictions has been shaken off, and while it is in the highest state called mastery, the stream of discriminative cognition becomes stainless.
That unwavering discriminative knowledge is the means to removal.

children.text: tato mithyājñānasya dagdhabījabhāvopagamaḥ punaścāprasava ity eṣa mokṣasya mārgo hānasyopāya iti ||
children.translated_text: Thereafter false knowledge comes to the condition of a burnt seed, and there is no further production: this is the path of liberation, the means to removal.
“Of that” refers back to the knowledge that has arisen.

children.text: saptadhetyaśuddhyāvaraṇamalāpagamāc cittasya pratyayāntarānutpāde sati saptaprakāraiva prajñā vivekino bhavati ||
children.translated_text: “Sevenfold”: when the impurity, covering, and dirt of the mind have gone away, and no other cognition arises, the insight of the discriminating person is of exactly seven kinds.
That is as follows:

children.text: parijñātaṃ heyaṃ nāsya punaḥ parijñeyam asti ||
children.translated_text: What is to be removed has been fully known; there is nothing further of it to be fully known.

children.text: kṣīṇā heyahetavo na punar eteṣāṃ kṣetavyam asti ||
children.translated_text: The causes of what is to be removed have been exhausted; there is nothing further of them to be exhausted.
Removal has been directly realized through the samādhi of cessation.
The means to removal, whose form is discriminative knowledge, has been cultivated.
This fourfold liberation of insight is connected with what is to be done.
But the liberation of the mind is threefold.
The intellect has fulfilled its authority.

children.text: guṇā giriśikharakūṭacyutā iva grāvāṇo niravasthānāḥ svakāraṇe pralayābhimukhāḥ saha tenāstaṃ gacchanti ||
children.translated_text: The guṇas, like stones fallen from the peak of a mountain, having no place to stand and tending toward dissolution into their own cause, set together with it.

children.text: na caiṣāṃ pravilīnānāṃ punar astyutpādaḥ prayojanābhāvād iti ||
children.translated_text: And when they have dissolved, there is no arising of them again, because there is no purpose for it.

children.text: etasyām avasthāyāṃ guṇasaṃbandhātītaḥ svarūpamātrajyotir amalaḥ kevalī puruṣa iti ||
children.translated_text: In this state, <s>puruṣa</s>, beyond relation with the guṇas, is pure, solitary, and luminous only as its own nature.

children.text: etāṃ saptavidhāṃ prāntabhūmiprajñām anupaśyan puruṣaḥ kuśala ity ākhyāyate ||
children.translated_text: Seeing this sevenfold insight at the final stage, <s>puruṣa</s> is called skillful.

children.text: pratiprasave 'pi cittasya muktaḥ kuśala ity eva bhavati guṇātītatvād iti ||
children.translated_text: Even when the mind is reabsorbed, it remains liberated and is still called skillful, because it has gone beyond the guṇas.
Thus discriminative knowledge, the means to removal, is established.

children.text: na ca siddhir antareṇa sādhanam ityetad ārabhyate ||
children.translated_text: And there is no accomplishment without a means; therefore this is begun.
The eight limbs of yoga are about to be set forth.

children.text: teṣām anuṣṭhānāt pañcaparvaṇo viparyayasyāśuddhirūpasya kṣayo nāśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: From the practice of these, there is the wasting away, the destruction, of the fivefold error whose form is impurity.
When that has wasted away, right knowledge becomes manifest.

children.text: yathā yathā ca sādhanāny anuṣṭhīyante tathā tathā tanutvam aśuddhir āpadyate ||
children.translated_text: In whatever way the means are practiced, in just that way impurity becomes attenuated.

children.text: yathā yathā ca kṣīyate tathā tathā kṣayakramānurodhinī jñānasyāpi dīptir vivardhate ||
children.translated_text: And in whatever way it is diminished, in just that way the brilliance of knowledge also increases, following the order of its diminution.

children.text: sā khalv eṣā vivṛddhiḥ prakarṣam anubhavaty ā vivekakhyāteḥ ||
children.translated_text: This increase indeed reaches its culmination in discriminative knowledge.
That is, up to the knowledge of the true nature of the guṇas and <s>puruṣa</s>.
Practice of the limbs of yoga is the cause of separation from impurity, as an axe is the cause of separation for what is to be cut.

children.text: vivekakhyātes tu prāptikāraṇaṃ yathā dharmaḥ sukhasya nānyathā kāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: But it is the cause for attaining discriminative knowledge, just as <s>dharma</s> is the cause of happiness, and not a cause in any other way.
How many such causes are there in the śāstra?
It says: just nine.
That is as follows:
Origination, maintenance, manifestation, transformation, cognition, attainment,
separation, otherness, and support: cause is remembered as ninefold.
Thus.
Among these, the mind is the cause of origination for cognition.
Being for the sake of <s>puruṣa</s> is the cause of maintenance for the mind, as food is for the body.
As light is the cause of manifestation for form, so knowledge of form is a cause of manifestation.
Another object is the cause of transformation for the mind, as fire is for what is to be cooked.
Knowledge of smoke is the cause of cognition for knowledge of fire.
Practice of the limbs of yoga is the cause of attainment for discriminative knowledge.
That same practice is the cause of separation from impurity.
The cause of otherness is like the goldsmith for gold.

children.text: evam ekasya strīpratyayasyāvidyā mūḍhatve dveṣo duḥkhatve rāgaḥ sukhatve tattvajñānaṃ mādhyasthye ||
children.translated_text: In the same way, with regard to a single cognition of a woman, there is ignorance when it is delusion, aversion when it is suffering, attachment when it is pleasure, and true knowledge when there is neutrality.

children.text: dhṛtikāraṇaṃ śarīram indriyāṇām tāni ca tasya ||
children.translated_text: The body is the cause of support for the senses, and they are also the cause of support for it.

children.text: mahābhūtāni śarīrāṇām tāni ca parasparaṃ sarveṣām ||
children.translated_text: The great elements are the cause of support for bodies, and they are also mutually so for all of them.
And animals, humans, and divine beings are mutually for one another's sake.
Thus there are nine causes.

children.text: tāni ca yathāsaṃbhavaṃ padārthāntareṣv api yojyāni ||
children.translated_text: And these should also be applied, as appropriate, to other categories.

children.text: yogāṅgānuṣṭhānaṃ tu dvidhaiva kāraṇatvaṃ labhata iti ||
children.translated_text: But the practice of the limbs of yoga obtains causality in only two ways.
There the limbs of yoga are determined.

children.text: yathākramam eṣām anuṣṭhānaṃ svarūpaṃ ca vakṣyāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: We shall state their practice in order and also their own nature.
There:

children.text: tatrāhiṃsā sarvathā sarvadā sarvabhūtānām anabhidrohaḥ uttare ca yamaniyamās tanmūlās tatsiddhiparatayaiva tatpratipādanāya pratipādyante tadavadātarūpakaraṇāyaivopādīyante ||
children.translated_text: Here, <s>ahiṃsā</s> is non-injury toward all beings, in every way and at all times. And the following yamas and niyamas have this as their root; they are taught only for the sake of its accomplishment, and they are undertaken only in order to bring about its stainless form.
And so it has been said:

children.text: sa khalvayaṃ brāhmaṇo yathā yathā vratāni bahūni samāditsate tathā tathā pramādakṛtebhyo hiṃsānidānebhyo nivartamānas tām evāvadātarūpām ahiṃsāṃ karoti ||
children.translated_text: Indeed, in whatever way this <s>brāhmaṇa</s> undertakes many vows, in just that way, turning away from the causes of injury that arise through negligence, he makes that very <s>ahiṃsā</s> stainless in form.
<s>Satya</s> is speech and mind in accordance with the object as it is.

children.text: yathā dṛṣṭaṃ yathānumitaṃ yathā śrutaṃ tathā vāṅ manaśceti ||
children.translated_text: As something has been seen, as it has been inferred, and as it has been heard, so should speech and mind be.

children.text: paratra svabodhasaṃkrāntaye vāg uktā sā yadi na vañcitā bhrāntā vā pratipattibandhyā vā bhaved iti ||
children.translated_text: Speech is uttered in order to transmit one's understanding to another; it is such if it is not deceptive, mistaken, or barren of comprehension.
This is undertaken for the benefit of all beings, not for the harming of beings.

children.text: yadi caivam apyabhidhīyamānā bhūtopaghātaparaiva syān na satyaṃ bhavet pāpam eva bhavet ||
children.translated_text: And if, even when spoken in this way, it were directed only toward harm to beings, it would not be truth; it would be only sin.

children.text: tena puṇyābhāsena puṇyapratirūpakeṇa kaṣṭaṃ tamaḥ prāpnuyāt ||
children.translated_text: By that semblance of merit, that counterfeit of merit, one would reach painful darkness.
Therefore, after examining it, one should speak the truth that is beneficial to all beings.

children.text: steyam aśāstrapūrvakaṃ dravyāṇāṃ parataḥ svīkaraṇaṃ tatpratiṣedhaḥ punar aspṛhārūpam asteyam iti ||
children.translated_text: Theft is the taking of others' goods without scriptural sanction; its prohibition, again, whose form is freedom from craving, is called <s>asteya</s>.
<s>Brahmacarya</s> is restraint of the guarded sexual organ.

children.text: viṣayāṇām arjanarakṣaṇakṣayasaṅgahiṃsādoṣadarśanād asvīkaraṇam aparigraha iti ete yamāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Non-acceptance of objects, because one sees the faults in their acquisition, protection, loss, attachment, and injury, is <s>aparigraha</s>. These are the yamas.
But they are:
Here <s>ahiṃsā</s> may be limited by class.
For a fisherman, injury is only toward fish, not elsewhere.
That same injury may be limited by place.
For example, 'I shall not kill at a sacred ford.'
That same injury may be limited by time.
For example, 'I shall not kill on the fourteenth lunar day, nor on an auspicious day.'
That same injury, when one has desisted from these three, may be limited by occasion.
For example, 'I shall kill for the sake of gods and <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, not otherwise.'

children.text: yathā ca kṣatriyāṇāṃ yuddha eva hiṃsā nānyatreti ||
children.translated_text: And similarly, for <s>kṣatriyas</s>, injury is only in battle and not elsewhere.

children.text: ebhir jātideśakālasamayair anavacchinnā ahiṃsādayaḥ sarvathaiva paripālanīyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Ahiṃsā</s> and the others, when not limited by these conditions of class, place, time, and occasion, are to be observed absolutely in every way.

children.text: sarvabhūmiṣu sarvaviṣayeṣu sarvathaivāviditavyabhicārāḥ sārvabhaumā mahāvratam ity ucyante ||
children.translated_text: When they are without known exception on all grounds, toward all objects, and in every way, they are called the universal great vow.

children.text: tatra śaucaṃ mṛjjalādijanitaṃ medhyābhyavaharaṇādi ca bāhyam ||
children.translated_text: Among these, external purity is that produced by clay, water, and the like, and also by eating what is fit to be eaten.
Internal purity is the washing away of the impurities of the mind.
Contentment is the absence of a desire to acquire more than the means that are at hand.
Austerity is the endurance of pairs of opposites.

children.text: dvandvaśca jighatsāpipāse śītoṣṇe sthānāsane kāṣṭhamaunākāramaune ca ||
children.translated_text: The pairs of opposites are hunger and thirst, cold and heat, standing and sitting, and also the forms of silence that are like a block of wood and true silence.
And the vows belonging to these, as appropriate, are the <s>kṛcchra</s>, <s>cāndrāyaṇa</s>, <s>sāṃtapana</s>, and the like.
<s>Svādhyāya</s> is the study of the śāstras on liberation, or the repetition of the praṇava.
<s>Īśvarapraṇidhāna</s> is the offering of all actions to him, the supreme teacher.
Whether lying on a bed or seat, or walking on the road,
being well, with the net of discursive thoughts exhausted,
seeing the destruction of the seed of saṃsāra,
one should be eternally liberated and a partaker of immortal enjoyment.
With reference to this it has been said:
From that there is also the attainment of inward consciousness and the absence of obstacles.
Regarding these yamas and niyamas:

children.text: yadāsya brāhmaṇasya hiṃsādayo vitarkā jāyeran haniṣyāmy aham apakāriṇam nṛtam api vakṣyāmi dravyam apy asya svīkariṣyāmi dāreṣu cāsya vyavāyī bhaviṣyāmi parigraheṣu cāsya svāmī bhaviṣyāmīti ||
children.translated_text: When harmful thoughts such as injury arise in this <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, such as, 'I will kill the one who has wronged me; I will also speak falsehood; I will also take his property; I will have intercourse with his wives; and I will become master of his possessions,'
then, being afflicted by the blazing fever of thoughts tending toward the wrong path, he should cultivate their opposites.

children.text: ghoreṣu saṃsārāṅgāreṣu pacyamānena mayā śaraṇam upāgataḥ sarvabhūtābhayapradānena yogadharmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: He should think, 'While I am being cooked in the terrible embers of saṃsāra, I have taken refuge in the yoga-dharma, through giving fearlessness to all beings.'

children.text: sa khalv ahaṃ tyaktvā vitarkān punas tān ādadānas tulyaḥ śvavṛtteneti bhāvayet ||
children.translated_text: Indeed, if I, having abandoned these harmful thoughts, take them up again, I am like a dog in conduct; so he should reflect.

children.text: yathā śvā vāntāvalehī tathā tyaktasya punar ādadāna ityevamādi sūtrāntareṣv api yojyam ||
children.translated_text: Just as a dog licks up what has been vomited, so is one who again takes up what has been abandoned. This and similar reasoning should also be applied in other sūtras.

children.text: tatra hiṃsā tāvat kṛtā kāritānumoditeti tridhā ||
children.translated_text: There, injury first is threefold: done by oneself, caused to be done, and approved.
Each one again is threefold.

children.text: lobhena māṃsacarmārthena krodhenāpakṛtam aneneti mohena dharmo me bhaviṣyatīti ||
children.translated_text: It may be through greed, for the sake of meat and hide; through anger, thinking, 'He has wronged me'; or through delusion, thinking, 'It will be my dharma.'
Greed, anger, and delusion again are threefold: mild, moderate, and intense.
Thus there are twenty-seven divisions of injury.
Again, the mild, moderate, and intense are threefold.
They are mild-mild, moderate-mild, and intense-mild.
Likewise, there are mild-moderate, moderate-moderate, and intense-moderate.
Likewise, there are mild-intense, moderate-intense, and extremely intense.
Thus violence has eighty-one varieties.

children.text: sā punar niyamavikalpasamuccayabhedād asaṃkhyeyā prāṇabhṛdbhedasyāparisaṃkhyeyatvād iti ||
children.translated_text: And that again is innumerable because of distinctions of restriction, option, and combination, since the distinctions among living beings cannot be counted.
The same should be applied also to falsehood and the rest.

children.text: te khalvamī vitarkā duḥkhājñānānantaphalā iti pratipakṣabhāvanam ||
children.translated_text: These contrary thoughts, then, have pain, ignorance, and endless result: this is the cultivation of the opposite.

children.text: duḥkham ajñānaṃ cānantaṃ phalaṃ yeṣām iti pratipakṣabhāvanam ||
children.translated_text: Their result is pain and ignorance, and it is endless: this is the cultivation of the opposite.

children.text: tathā ca hiṃsakas tāvat prathamaṃ vadhyasya vīryam ākṣipati tataśca śastrādinipātena duḥkhayati tato jīvitād api mocayati tato vīryākṣepād asya cetanācetanam upakaraṇaṃ kṣīṇavīryaṃ bhavati duḥkhotpādān narakatiryakpretādiṣu duḥkham anubhavati jīvitavyaparopaṇāt pratikṣaṇaṃ ca jīvitātyaye vartamāno maraṇam icchann api duḥkhavipākasya niyatavipākavedanīyatvāt kathaṃcid evocchvasati ||
children.translated_text: For example, the violent man first strikes down the strength of the one to be killed; then, by the fall of a weapon and the like, he causes him pain; then he also releases him from life. Because of the striking down of strength, his own animate and inanimate instruments become weakened in strength. Because he produces pain, he experiences pain in hells, animal births, ghost states, and the like. Because he cuts off life, while at every moment he remains in danger of losing life, and though he desires death, he somehow keeps breathing, since the ripening of painful result is fixed and must be experienced.

children.text: yadi ca kathaṃcit puṇyāvāpagatā hiṃsā bhavet tatra sukhaprāptau bhaved alpāyur iti ||
children.translated_text: And if somehow violence should be accompanied by an influx of merit, then, when happiness is obtained there, he would be short-lived.
In the same way this should be applied, as appropriate, also to falsehood and the rest.

children.text: evaṃ vitarkāṇāṃ cāmum evānugataṃ vipākam aniṣṭaṃ bhāvayan na vitarkeṣu manaḥ praṇidadhīta ||
children.translated_text: Thus, contemplating this very undesirable ripening that follows upon contrary thoughts, one should not direct the mind toward contrary thoughts.

children.text: pratipakṣabhāvanāhetor heyā vitarkā yadāsya syur aprasavadharmāṇas tadā tatkṛtam aiśvaryaṃ yoginaḥ siddhisūcakaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: When the contrary thoughts to be abandoned through the cause that is cultivation of the opposite become, for him, incapable of arising, then the mastery produced by that becomes an indicator of the yogin's accomplishment.
That is as follows:
It exists for all living beings.
If he says, 'May he become righteous,' he becomes righteous.
If he says, 'May you attain heaven,' he attains heaven.
His speech becomes unfailing.
Jewels from every quarter present themselves to him.

children.text: yasya lābhād apratighān guṇān utkarṣayati siddhaśca vineyeṣu jñānam ādhātuṃ samartho bhavatīti ||
children.translated_text: By gaining this, he raises qualities without obstruction; and, being accomplished, he becomes capable of placing knowledge in those to be trained.
For him there arises:

children.text: ko 'ham āsaṃ katham aham āsaṃ kiṃsvid idaṃ ke vā bhaviṣyāmaḥ kathaṃ vā bhaviṣyāma ity evam asya pūrvāntaparāntamadhyeṣv ātmabhāvajijñāsā svarūpeṇopāvartate ||
children.translated_text: 'Who was I? How was I? What is this? Who shall we be? And how shall we be?' In this way, the desire to know his own state in the earlier end, the later end, and the middle arises for him in its own form.
These are the accomplishments that come from firmness in the yamas.
We shall speak of those connected with the niyamas.

children.text: svāṅge jugupsāyāṃ śaucam ārabhamāṇaḥ kāyāvadyadarśī kāyānabhiṣvaṅgī yatir bhavati ||
children.translated_text: When disgust toward one's own body arises, one who undertakes purity, seeing the faults of the body and not clinging to the body, becomes an ascetic.

children.text: kiṃca parair asaṃsargaḥ kāyasvabhāvāvalokī svam api kāyaṃ jihāsur mṛjjalādibhir ākṣālayann api kāyaśuddhim apaśyan kathaṃ parakāyair atyantam evāprayataiḥ saṃsṛjyeta ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, there is non-contact with others. Seeing the nature of the body and wishing to abandon even his own body, and not seeing purity of the body even though he washes it with clay, water, and the like, how could he come into contact with other bodies, which are utterly impure?
Moreover:
'They arise' is the completion of the sentence.

children.text: śuceḥ sattvaśuddhis tataḥ saumanasyaṃ tata aikāgryaṃ tata indriyajayas tataścātmadarśanayogyatvaṃ buddhisattvasya bhavatīty etac chaucasthairyād adhigamyata iti ||
children.translated_text: From purity there is purification of <s>sattva</s>; from that, cheerfulness; from that, one-pointedness; from that, mastery of the senses; and from that, fitness of the intellect's <s>sattva</s> for seeing the self. This is attained from firmness in purity.
And so it has been said:

children.text: yacca kāmasukhaṃ loke yacca divyaṃ mahat sukham
children.translated_text: Whatever pleasure of desire exists in the world, and whatever great heavenly pleasure there is,
these are not worth a sixteenth part of the pleasure of the destruction of thirst.
Thus.
Austerity, even while it is being performed, destroys the impurity and dirt that form an obstruction.
When the dirt that is that obstruction has gone away, there is bodily accomplishment such as minuteness and the rest.
Likewise there is accomplishment of the senses, such as hearing and seeing at a distance.

children.text: devā ṛṣayaḥ siddhāśca svādhyāyaśīlasya darśanaṃ gacchanti kārye cāsya vartanta iti ||
children.translated_text: Gods, seers, and perfected beings come into the presence of one who is devoted to study, and they attend to his business.

children.text: īśvarārpitasarvabhāvasya samādhisiddhir yayā sarvam īpsitam avitathaṃ jānāti deśāntare dehāntare kālāntare ca ||
children.translated_text: For one whose entire state of being is offered to <s>Īśvara</s>, there is accomplishment in <s>samādhi</s>, by which he knows without error everything desired, in another place, another body, and another time.
From that, his wisdom knows things as they really are.
The yamas and niyamas have been stated together with their accomplishments.
We shall speak of posture and the rest.
There:

children.text: tad yathā padmāsanaṃ vīrāsanaṃ bhadrāsanaṃ svastikaṃ daṇḍāsanaṃ sopāśrayaṃ paryaṅkaṃ krauñcaniṣadanaṃ hastiniṣadanam uṣṭraniṣadanaṃ samasaṃsthānaṃ sthirasukhaṃ yathāsukhaṃ cety evamādīni ||
children.translated_text: That is, <s>padmāsana</s>, <s>vīrāsana</s>, <s>bhadrāsana</s>, <s>svastika</s>, <s>daṇḍāsana</s>, the supported posture, the couch posture, the heron-sitting posture, the elephant-sitting posture, the camel-sitting posture, the evenly arranged posture, the steady-and-easy posture, the posture according to comfort, and others of this kind.
'It is' is the completion of the sentence.
Posture is perfected through cessation of effort, by which there is no trembling of the limbs.

children.text: anante vā samāpannaṃ cittam āsanaṃ nirvartayatīti ||
children.translated_text: Or, the mind absorbed in <s>Ananta</s> brings posture to completion.
From mastery of posture, one is not overcome by pairs of opposites such as cold and heat.
When mastery of posture exists, inhalation is the drawing in of external air.
Exhalation is the expelling of air from the belly.
The interruption of the movement of these two, the absence of both, is breath regulation.
Where there is absence of movement preceded by exhalation, that is external.
Where there is absence of movement preceded by inhalation, that is internal.
The third has the function of stoppage, where the absence of both occurs through a single effort.

children.text: yathā tapte nyastam upale jalaṃ sarvataḥ saṃkocam āpadyate tathā dvayor yugapadgatyabhāva iti ||
children.translated_text: Just as water placed on a heated stone contracts on every side, so too there is the simultaneous absence of movement of both.

children.text: trayo 'py ete deśena paridṛṣṭā iyān asya viṣayo deśa iti ||
children.translated_text: All three of these are observed with respect to place: ‘This much is its range in place.’
They are observed with respect to time, meaning that they are delimited by determining the measure of moments.

children.text: saṃkhyābhiḥ paridṛṣṭā etāvadbhiḥ śvāsapraśvāsaiḥ prathama udghātas tadvan nigṛhītasyaitāvadbhir dvitīya udghāta evaṃ tṛtīyaḥ evaṃ mṛdur evaṃ madhya evaṃ tīvra iti saṃkhyāparidṛṣṭaḥ ||
children.translated_text: They are observed by numbers: the first exertion is with so many inhalations and exhalations; likewise, for one who has restrained it, the second exertion is with so many, and so the third; thus it is mild, thus medium, thus intense. In this way it is observed by number.

children.text: sa khalv ayam evam abhyasto dīrghasūkṣmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: This, then, when practiced in this manner, becomes long and subtle.
It is directed toward an external object, observed by place, time, and number.
Likewise it is directed toward an internal object, observed in that sphere.
In both ways it is long and subtle.
Preceded by that, through mastery of the stages, the absence of movement in both is the fourth <s>prāṇāyāma</s>.

children.text: tṛtīyas tu viṣayānālocito gatyabhāvaḥ sakṛdārabdha eva deśakālasaṃkhyābhiḥ paridṛṣṭo dīrghasūkṣmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But the third is an absence of movement whose objects have not been contemplated; once begun, it is observed by place, time, and number, and is long and subtle.

children.text: caturthas tu śvāsapraśvāsayor viṣayāvadhāraṇāt krameṇa bhūmijayād ubhayākṣepapūrvako gatyabhāvaścaturthaḥ prāṇāyāma ity ayaṃ viśeṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The fourth, however, is the absence of movement of inhalation and exhalation, preceded by the suspension of both, through the determination of their object and, gradually, through mastery of the stages. This is the distinction in the fourth <s>prāṇāyāma</s>.

children.text: prāṇāyāmān abhyasyato 'sya yoginaḥ kṣīyate vivekajñānāvaraṇīyaṃ karma ||
children.translated_text: For this yogin who practices <s>prāṇāyāma</s>, the karma that covers discriminative knowledge is diminished.
That is what they declare:

children.text: mahāmohamayenendrajālena prakāśaśīlaṃ sattvam āvṛtya tad evākārye niyuṅkta iti ||
children.translated_text: Having covered <s>sattva</s>, whose nature is illumination, with the magic net made of great delusion, it directs that very <s>sattva</s> toward what ought not to be done.

children.text: tad asya prakāśāvaraṇaṃ karma saṃskāranibandhanaṃ prāṇāyāmābhyāsād durbalaṃ bhavati pratikṣaṇaṃ ca kṣīyate ||
children.translated_text: That karma of his, which covers illumination and is bound up with latent impressions, becomes weak through the practice of <s>prāṇāyāma</s>, and at every moment it is diminished.
And so it has been said:

children.text: tapo na paraṃ prāṇāyāmāt tato viśuddhir malānāṃ dīptiśca jñānasyeti ||
children.translated_text: There is no austerity higher than <s>prāṇāyāma</s>; from it comes the purification of impurities and the brightness of knowledge.
Moreover:

children.text: prāṇāyāmābhyāsād eva pracchardanavidhāraṇābhyāṃ vā prāṇasya iti vacanāt ||
children.translated_text: This follows from the statement, ‘or by exhalation and retention of the breath,’ since it is precisely from the practice of <s>prāṇāyāma</s>.
Now, what is <s>pratyāhāra</s>?

children.text: svaviṣayasaṃprayogābhāve cittasvarūpānukāra iveti cittanirodhe cittavan niruddhānīndriyāṇi netarendriyajayavad upāyāntaram apekṣante ||
children.translated_text: In the absence of contact with their own objects, there is, as it were, conformity to the nature of the mind: when the mind is restrained, the senses, like the mind, are restrained and do not require another means, as in other forms of sense-mastery.

children.text: yathā madhukararājaṃ makṣikā utpatantam anūtpatanti niviśamānam anuniviśante tathendriyāṇi cittanirodhe niruddhānīty eṣa pratyāhāraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Just as bees fly up after the king bee when he flies up and settle down after him when he settles, so the senses are restrained when the mind is restrained. This is <s>pratyāhāra</s>.
Some say that mastery of the senses is not being addicted to sound and the other objects.

children.text: saktir vyasanaṃ vyasyaty enaṃ śreyasa iti ||
children.translated_text: Attachment is addiction, because it throws one away from the highest good.
A proper understanding is one that is not contradictory.
Others say it is contact with sound and the other objects according to one’s own will.

children.text: rāgadveṣābhāve sukhaduḥkhaśūnyaṃ śabdādijñānam indriyajaya iti kecit ||
children.translated_text: Some say that sense-mastery is cognition of sound and the other objects, empty of pleasure and pain because attraction and aversion are absent.
<s>Jaigīṣavya</s> says that, because of one-pointedness of mind, it is simply non-apprehension.

children.text: tataśca paramā tviyaṃ vaśyatā yac cittanirodhe niruddhānīndriyāṇi netarendriyajayavat prayatnakṛtam upāyāntaram apekṣante yogina iti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore this is the supreme subjugation: when the mind is restrained, the senses are restrained and do not require some other means produced by effort for the yogin, as other kinds of sense-mastery do.

children.text: iti śrīpātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre sādhananirdeśo nāma dvitīyaḥ pādaḥ samāptaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the venerable Pātañjala <s>Sāṃkhya</s>-teaching, in the yoga śāstra, the second pāda, called the Instruction on Practice, is complete.

children.text: nābhicakre hṛdayapuṇḍarīke mūrdhni jyotiṣi nāsikāgre jihvāgre ity evamādiṣu deśeṣu bāhye vā viṣaye cittasya vṛttimātreṇa bandha iti dhāraṇā ||
children.translated_text: Binding the mind by means of nothing but its activity to places such as the navel-wheel, the heart-lotus, the crown of the head, the light, the tip of the nose, the tip of the tongue, and so on, or to an external object, is <s>dhāraṇā</s>.

children.text: buddhisattvaṃ prakhyāśīlaṃ samānasattvopanibandhane rajastamasī vaśīkṛtya sattvapuruṣānyatāpratyayena pariṇatam ||
children.translated_text: The clarity-natured <s>sattva</s> of the intellect, having brought <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> under control in connection with a <s>sattva</s> of the same kind, is transformed through the cognition of the difference between <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>.

children.text: tasmāc ca sattvāt pariṇāmino 'tyantavidharmā śuddho 'nyaścitimātrarūpaḥ puruṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And distinct from that changing <s>sattva</s>, utterly different in nature, is <s>puruṣa</s>, pure, other, and consisting only of consciousness.

children.text: tayor atyantāsaṃkīrṇayoḥ pratyayāviśeṣo bhogaḥ puruṣasya darśitaviṣayatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Enjoyment is the non-distinction of cognition between those two, although they are utterly unmixed, because the object has been presented to <s>puruṣa</s>.
That cognition of enjoyment, because <s>sattva</s> exists for the sake of another, is something seen.

children.text: yas tu tasmād viśiṣṭaścitimātrarūpo 'nyaḥ pauruṣeyaḥ pratyayas tatra saṃyamāt puruṣaviṣayā prajñā jāyate ||
children.translated_text: But the cognition that is distinct from that, consisting only of consciousness and belonging to <s>puruṣa</s>, is different; through <s>saṃyama</s> on that, insight whose object is <s>puruṣa</s> arises.

children.text: na ca puruṣapratyayena buddhisattvātmanā puruṣo dṛśyate puruṣa eva taṃ pratyayaṃ svātmāvalambanaṃ paśyati ||
children.translated_text: And <s>puruṣa</s> is not seen by the cognition of <s>puruṣa</s> when that cognition has the nature of the intellect's <s>sattva</s>; rather, <s>puruṣa</s> itself sees that cognition, which rests on its own self.
For so it has been said:
By what, dear one, could one know the knower?
Thus.
From intuitive illumination there is knowledge of what is subtle, hidden, remote, past, and future.
From the auditory faculty there is hearing of divine sound.
From sensation there is attainment of divine touch.
From the mirror-like faculty there is awareness of divine form.
From the faculty of report there is knowledge of divine smell.
These arise constantly.
Those, beginning with intuitive illumination, when they arise in a mind that is concentrated, are impediments, because they oppose the vision of that goal.
When they arise in a mind that has emerged from concentration, they are perfections.

children.text: lolībhūtasya manaso 'pratiṣṭhasya śarīre karmāśayavaśād bandhaḥ pratiṣṭhety arthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For a mind that has become unsteady and has no fixed support, its bondage in a body through the force of the store of karma is what is meant by its establishment.

children.text: tasya karmaṇo bandhakāraṇasya śaithilyaṃ samādhibalād bhavati ||
children.translated_text: The loosening of that karma, the cause of bondage, comes about through the power of <s>samādhi</s>.

children.text: pracārasaṃvedanaṃ ca samādhijam eva karmabandhakṣayāt svacittasya pracārasaṃvedanāc ca yogī cittaṃ svaśarīrān niṣkṛṣya śarīrāntareṣu nikṣipati ||
children.translated_text: And the perception of its movement is also born of <s>samādhi</s>; from the destruction of karmic bondage and from perceiving the movement of his own mind, the yogin draws the mind out of his own body and deposits it in other bodies.
And the senses follow the mind.

children.text: yathā madhukararājānaṃ makṣikā utpatantam anūtpatanti niviśamānam anuniviśante tathendriyāṇi paraśarīrāveśe cittam anuvidhīyanta iti ||
children.translated_text: Just as bees fly up after the king bee when he flies up and settle down after him when he settles, so, when the mind enters another body, the senses follow it.
Life is the whole activity of the senses, characterized by <s>prāṇa</s> and the others.
Its action is fivefold.

children.text: prāṇo mukhanāsikāgatir ā hṛdayavṛttiḥ samaṃ nayanāt samāna ā nābhivṛttir apanayanād apāna ā pādatalavṛttir unnayanād udāna ā śirovṛttir vyāpī vyāna iti ||
children.translated_text: <s>Prāṇa</s> moves through the mouth and nose and functions as far as the heart; because it leads evenly, <s>samāna</s> functions as far as the navel; because it carries away, <s>apāna</s> functions as far as the soles of the feet; because it raises upward, <s>udāna</s> functions as far as the head; and because it pervades, <s>vyāna</s> is all-pervasive.
Among these, <s>prāṇa</s> is the chief one.

children.text: udānajayāj jalapaṅkakaṇṭakādiṣvasaṅga utkrāntiśca prāyaṇakāle bhavati tāṃ vaśitvena pratipadyate ||
children.translated_text: Through mastery of <s>udāna</s>, non-adhesion in water, mud, thorns, and the like, and also departure at the time of death, come about; he attains control over that.
One who has mastered <s>samāna</s>, having made an inflation of heat, blazes.
Space is the foundation of all auditory faculties and of all sounds.
As has been said:
For those who hear in the same place, all have hearing of one and the same place.

children.text: tac caitad ākāśasya liṅgam anāvaraṇaṃ coktam ||
children.translated_text: And this has been stated as the mark of space, namely non-obstruction.
Likewise, from the observation that the incorporeal is unobstructed, the all-pervasiveness of space is also well known.

children.text: śabdagrahaṇānumitaṃ śrotraṃ badhirābadhirayor ekaḥ śabdaṃ gṛhṇāty aparo na gṛhṇātīti ||
children.translated_text: The auditory faculty is inferred from the apprehension of sound: of a deaf person and a non-deaf person, one grasps a sound and the other does not.
Therefore the auditory faculty alone has sound as its object.

children.text: śrotrākāśayoḥ saṃbandhe kṛtasaṃyamasya yogino divyaṃ śrotraṃ pravartate ||
children.translated_text: For a yogin who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on the relation between the auditory faculty and space, divine hearing comes into operation.

children.text: yatra kāyas tatrākāśaṃ tasyāvakāśadānāt kāyasya tena saṃbandhaḥ prāptiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Wherever there is a body, there is space; because it gives room to the body, the body's relation to it is contact or attainment.

children.text: tatra kṛtasaṃyamo jitvā tatsaṃbandhaṃ laghuṣu vā tūlādiṣv ā paramāṇubhyaḥ samāpattiṃ labdhvā jitasaṃbandho laghur bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Having performed <s>saṃyama</s> there, having mastered that relation, or having gained absorption in light things such as cotton, down to atoms, he becomes light, having mastered the relation.

children.text: laghutvāc ca jale pādābhyāṃ viharati tatas tūrṇanābhitantumātre vihṛtya raśmiṣu viharati ||
children.translated_text: And because of lightness he moves with his feet upon water; then, having moved upon a mere spider's thread, he moves upon rays of light.
Thereafter he has movement through space as he wishes.

children.text: śarīrād bahir manaso vṛttilābho videhā nāma dhāraṇā ||
children.translated_text: The acquisition of a mental activity outside the body is the <s>dhāraṇā</s> called bodiless.

children.text: sā yadi śarīrapratiṣṭhasya manaso bahirvṛttimātreṇa bhavati sā kalpitety ucyate ||
children.translated_text: If that occurs merely as an external activity of a mind established in the body, it is called imagined.

children.text: yā tu śarīranirapekṣā bahirbhūtasyaiva manaso bahirvṛttiḥ sā khalvakalpitā ||
children.translated_text: But the external activity of a mind that is independent of the body and itself outside it is indeed unimagined.

children.text: tatra kalpitayā sādhayanty akalpitāṃ mahāvidehām iti yathā paraśarīrāṇy āviśanti yoginaḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, by means of the imagined one, yogins accomplish the unimagined great bodiless state, just as they enter other bodies.

children.text: tataśca dhāraṇātaḥ prakāśātmano buddhisattvasya yad āvaraṇaṃ kleśakarmavipākatrayarajastamomūlaṃ tasya ca kṣayo bhavati ||
children.translated_text: And from that <s>dhāraṇā</s>, the covering of the intellect's <s>sattva</s>, whose nature is illumination and whose root is the threefold <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> of afflictions, karma, and fruition, is destroyed.

children.text: tatra pārthivādyāḥ śabdādayo viśeṣāḥ sahakārādibhir dharmaiḥ sthūlaśabdena paribhāṣitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, the particular qualities beginning with sound, belonging to earth and the other elements, together with assisting properties and so on, are designated by the word gross.
This is the first form of the elements.

children.text: dvitīyaṃ rūpaṃ svasāmānyaṃ mūrtir bhūmiḥ sneho jalaṃ vahnir uṣṇatā vāyuḥ praṇāmī sarvatogatir ākāśa ity etat svarūpaśabdenocyate ||
children.translated_text: The second form is their own general nature: solidity is earth, fluidity is water, heat is fire, what bends or moves in every direction is wind, and space is all-pervasive. This is called their intrinsic form.
Sound and the other particulars belong to this general nature.
And so it has been said:
For these things, which are joined by a single class-character, there is merely a distinction of properties.
Here, substance is the aggregate of universal and particular.
For an aggregate rests in two ways.

children.text: pratyastamitabhedāvayavānugataḥ śarīraṃ vṛkṣo yūthaṃ vanam iti ||
children.translated_text: An aggregate may be connected with parts whose differences have subsided, as in 'body,' 'tree,' 'herd,' or 'forest.'
An aggregate may also be connected with parts whose differences are taken up by the word.

children.text: ubhaye devamanuṣyāḥ samūhasya devā eko bhāgo manuṣyā dvitīyo bhāgaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In 'both gods and humans,' the gods are one part of the aggregate and humans the second part.
The aggregate is denoted by those very two.
And it is intended with both difference and non-difference.

children.text: āmrāṇāṃ vanaṃ brāhmaṇānāṃ saṃgha āmravaṇaṃ brāhmaṇasaṃgha iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, 'a forest of mango trees,' 'a group of brahmins,' 'mango-forest,' and 'brahmin-group.'
Again, it is of two kinds: one whose parts are established separately and one whose parts are not established separately.
An aggregate whose parts are established separately is a forest or a group.

children.text: ayutasiddhāvayavaḥ saṃghātaḥ śarīraṃ vṛkṣaḥ paramāṇur iti ||
children.translated_text: An aggregate whose parts are not established separately is a composite, such as a body, a tree, or an atom.
According to <s>Patañjali</s>, a substance is an aggregate connected with distinct parts that are not established separately.
This has been stated as intrinsic form.
Now, what is their subtle form?
The subtle element, the cause of the gross element.

children.text: tasyaiko 'vayavaḥ paramāṇuḥ sāmānyaviśeṣātmāyutasiddhāvayavabhedānugataḥ samudāya ity evaṃ sarvatanmātrāṇy etat tṛtīyam ||
children.translated_text: One part of it is the atom, having the nature of universal and particular, an aggregate connected with distinct parts that are not established separately. Thus all subtle elements are this third form.

children.text: atha bhūtānāṃ caturthaṃ rūpaṃ khyātikriyāsthitiśīlā guṇāḥ kāryasvabhāvānupātino 'nvayaśabdenoktāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now the fourth form of the elements is the qualities, whose nature is illumination, activity, and stability, following the nature of their effects; these are called continuity.

children.text: athaiṣa pañcamaṃ rūpam arthavattvaṃ bhogāpavargārthatā guṇeṣvanvayinī guṇās tanmātrabhūtabhautikeṣv iti sarvam arthavat ||
children.translated_text: Now their fifth form is purposiveness: being for the sake of experience and liberation. This inheres in the qualities, and the qualities inhere in the subtle elements, gross elements, and products of the elements; thus everything is purposeful.

children.text: teṣv idānīṃ bhūteṣu pañcasu pañcarūpeṣu saṃyamāt tasya tasya rūpasya svarūpadarśanaṃ jayaśca prādurbhavati ||
children.translated_text: Now, through <s>saṃyama</s> on those five elements in their five forms, vision of the intrinsic nature of each form and mastery over it arise for him.

children.text: tatra pañca bhūtasvarūpāṇi jitvā bhūtajayī bhavati ||
children.translated_text: There, having mastered the five intrinsic forms of the elements, he becomes one who has mastered the elements.

children.text: tajjayād vatsānusāriṇya iva gāvo 'sya saṃkalpānuvidhāyinyo bhūtaprakṛtayo bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: From mastery of them, the elemental natures become obedient to his intention, like cows following their calves.
There, <s>aṇimā</s>: he becomes minute.
<s>Laghimā</s>: he becomes light.
<s>Mahimā</s>: he becomes great.
<s>Prāpti</s>: even with the tip of his finger he touches the moon.

children.text: prākāmyam icchānabhighātaḥ bhūmāv unmajjati nimajjati yathodake ||
children.translated_text: <s>Prākāmya</s> is the non-obstruction of one’s wish: one emerges from the earth and sinks into it as into water.
<s>Vaśitva</s> is mastery: one gains control over the elements and their products, and is not subject to the control of others.
<s>Īśitṛtva</s> is lordship over the arising, disappearance, and arrangement of those things.

children.text: yatra kāmāvasāyitvaṃ satyasaṃkalpatā yathā saṃkalpas tathā bhūtaprakṛtīnām avasthānam ||
children.translated_text: Wherever there is fulfillment according to one’s desire, there is truth of resolve: just as the resolve is, so is the condition of the elemental natures.
And yet, even though he is capable, he does not bring about a reversal of things.
Why?

children.text: anyasya yatra kāmāvasāyinaḥ pūrvasiddhasya tathā bhūteṣu saṃkalpād iti ||
children.translated_text: Because in that matter there is the resolve, with respect to the elements, of another who has fulfillment according to desire and who has attained it earlier.
These are the eight lordly powers.
The perfection of the body will be explained below.

children.text: taddharmānabhighātaśca pṛthvī mūrtyā na niruṇaddhi yoginaḥ śarīrādikriyāṃ śilām apy anuviśatīti nāpaḥ snigdhāḥ kledayanti nāgnir uṣṇo dahati na vāyuḥ praṇāmī vahati ||
