children.translated_text: And there is non-obstruction by their properties: earth, by its solidity, does not obstruct the yogin’s bodily and other actions, for he even enters into stone; waters, though moist, do not wet him; fire, though hot, does not burn him; wind, though moving by bending forward, does not carry him away.

children.text: anāvaraṇātmake 'py ākāśe bhavaty āvṛtakāyaḥ siddhānām apy adṛśyo bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Even in space, whose nature is non-obstruction, he has a covered body and becomes invisible even to perfected beings.
He is beautiful, radiant, possessed of surpassing strength, and has a body as compact as a thunderbolt.

children.text: sāmānyaviśeṣātmā śabdādir grāhyaḥ teṣvindriyāṇāṃ vṛttir grahaṇam ||
children.translated_text: Sound and the rest, whose nature is both general and particular, are what is grasped; the activity of the senses with respect to them is grasping.

children.text: na ca tat sāmānyamātragrahaṇākāraṃ katham anālocitaḥ sa viṣayaviśeṣa indriyeṇa manasā vānuvyavasīyeteti ||
children.translated_text: And that activity does not have the form of grasping the universal alone; for how could a particular object, not first illuminated, be subsequently determined by the sense or by the mind?

children.text: svarūpaṃ punaḥ prakāśātmano buddhisattvasya sāmānyaviśeṣayor ayutasiddhāvayavabhedānugataḥ samūho dravyam indriyam ||
children.translated_text: Again, their own form is this: the sense-faculty is a substance, a composite that follows the distinction of parts inseparably established in the universal and particular, belonging to the intellect-<s>sattva</s> whose nature is illumination.
Their third form is egoity, characterized by <s>asmitā</s>.
The senses are the particulars of that universal.

children.text: caturthaṃ rūpaṃ vyavasāyātmakāḥ prakāśakriyāsthitiśīlā guṇā yeṣām indriyāṇi sāhaṃkārāṇi pariṇāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The fourth form is the <s>guṇas</s>, whose nature is determination, illumination, activity, and stability, of which the senses, together with egoity, are a transformation.

children.text: pañcamaṃ rūpaṃ guṇeṣu yad anugataṃ puruṣārthavattvam iti ||
children.translated_text: The fifth form is the fact, present throughout the <s>guṇas</s>, that they serve the purpose of <s>puruṣa</s>.

children.text: pañcasv eteṣv indriyarūpeṣu yathākramaṃ saṃyamastatra tatra jayaṃ kṛtvā pañcarūpajayād indriyajayaḥ prādurbhavati yoginaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When <s>saṃyama</s> is applied successively to these five forms of the senses, victory over each of them is achieved; from victory over the five forms, mastery of the senses appears for the yogin.
The unsurpassed attainment of speed by the body is swiftness like that of the mind.
The disembodied condition of the senses is the attainment of activity by bodiless senses with reference to the desired place, time, and object.
Mastery over every modification of nature is victory over <s>pradhāna</s>.
These three perfections are called honey-faced.
And these are obtained through victory over the five forms of the instruments.

children.text: nirdhūtarajastamomalasya buddhisattvasya pare vaiśāradye parasyāṃ vaśīkārasaṃjñāyāṃ vartamānasya sattvapuruṣānyatākhyātimātrarūpapratiṣṭhasya sarvabhāvādhiṣṭhātṛtvam ||
children.translated_text: For the intellect-<s>sattva</s> whose stain of <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> has been shaken off, abiding in supreme clarity, in the highest state called mastery, and established in the mere form of knowledge of the difference between <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>, there is lordship over all beings.

children.text: sarvātmāno guṇā vyavasāyavyavaseyātmakāḥ svāminaṃ kṣetrajñaṃ praty aśeṣadṛśyātmatvenopasthitā ity arthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is that the <s>guṇas</s>, whose nature is everything and which consist of determination and what is to be determined, stand before their master, the knower of the field, as the whole nature of the seen.

children.text: sarvajñātṛtvaṃ sarvātmanāṃ guṇānāṃ śāntoditāvyapadeśyadharmatvena vyavasthitānām akramopārūḍhaṃ vivekajaṃ jñānam ity artha iti ||
children.translated_text: Omniscience means discriminative knowledge, mounted all at once, of the <s>guṇas</s> in all their forms, established as possessing properties that are quiescent, arisen, and not yet nameable.

children.text: eṣā viśokā nāma siddhir yāṃ prāpya yogī sarvajñaḥ kṣīṇakleśabandhano vaśī viharati ||
children.translated_text: This is the perfection called sorrowless; having attained it, the yogin lives as omniscient, with the bonds of affliction destroyed, and as a master.
A perfection that belongs to another body is one born by birth.
Through herbs, in the abodes of the <s>asuras</s>, there is elixir-practice, and so on.
Through mantras there is travel through the sky and the attainment of minuteness and the other powers.

children.text: tapasā saṃkalpasiddhiḥ kāmarūpī yatra tatra kāmaga ity evamādi ||
children.translated_text: Through austerity there is accomplishment of resolve, becoming one who assumes any desired form and goes wherever he wishes, and so on.
The perfections born of <s>samādhi</s> have been explained.
Here, with respect to bodies and senses transformed into another species,
the disappearance of the previous transformation and the arising of the later transformation take place through the entrance of unprecedented constituent parts into them.

children.text: kāyendriyaprakṛtayaśca svaṃ svaṃ vikāram anugṛhṇanty āpūreṇa dharmādinimittam apekṣamāṇā iti ||
children.translated_text: And the natures of body and senses assist their own respective modifications by a filling-up, while awaiting an occasion such as <s>dharma</s>.

children.text: na hi dharmādinimittaṃ tatprayojakaṃ prakṛtīnāṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: For an occasion such as <s>dharma</s> is not what impels those natures.
The cause is not set in motion by the effect.

children.text: kathaṃ tarhi varaṇabhedas tu tataḥ kṣetrikavat ||
children.translated_text: How then? By the breaking of the obstruction from that, like a farmer.

children.text: yathā kṣetrikaḥ kedārād apāṃ pūraṇāt kedārāntaraṃ piplāvayiṣuḥ samaṃ nimnaṃ nimnataraṃ vā nāpaḥ pāṇināpakarṣaty āvaraṇaṃ tv āsāṃ bhinatti tasmin bhinne svayam evāpaḥ kedārāntaram āplāvayanti tathā dharmaḥ prakṛtīnām āvaraṇam adharmaṃ bhinatti tasmin bhinne svayam eva prakṛtayaḥ svaṃ vikāram āplāvayanti ||
children.translated_text: Just as a farmer, wishing to flood another field by filling water from one field, does not draw the waters by hand to level ground, lower ground, or still lower ground, but breaks their obstruction; when that has been broken, the waters themselves flood the other field. In the same way <s>dharma</s> breaks <s>adharma</s>, the obstruction to the natures; when that has been broken, the natures themselves flood their own modification.

children.text: yathā vā sa eva kṣetrikas tasminn eva kedāre na prabhavaty audakān bhaumān vā rasān dhānyamūlāny anupraveśayitum ||
children.translated_text: Or just as that very farmer, in that same field, is not able to make the watery or earthy juices enter the roots of the grain.
Here <s>Nandīśvara</s> and others should be cited as examples.
Conversely, too, <s>adharma</s> obstructs <s>dharma</s>.
And from that there is transformation into impurity.
There too <s>Nahuṣa</s> becoming a serpent and others should be cited as examples.

children.text: yadā tu yogī bahūn kāyān nirmimīte tadā kim ekamanaskās te bhavanty athānekamanaskā iti ||
children.translated_text: But when the yogin creates many bodies, are they possessed of one mind, or are they possessed of many minds?
Taking mere egoity as the material cause of mind, he creates constructed minds.
Therefore they are furnished with minds.

children.text: bahūnāṃ cittānāṃ katham ekacittābhiprāyapuraḥsarā pravṛttir iti sarvacittānāṃ prayojakaṃ cittam ekaṃ nirmimīte tataḥ pravṛttibhedaḥ ||
children.translated_text: How can many minds proceed with the intention of a single mind before them? For that reason he constructs one mind that impels all the minds; from that follows the difference in their activities.
The constructed mind is fivefold, since the perfections arise from birth, herbs, mantra, austerity, and <s>samādhi</s>.

children.text: tatra yad eva dhyānajaṃ cittaṃ tad evānāśayam ||
children.translated_text: Among these, precisely the mind born from meditation is without a latent deposit.
It alone has no deposit, no activity proceeding from attachment and the like.
Therefore there is no connection with merit and demerit for the yogin, because his afflictions have been exhausted.
But for the others there is a <s>karmāśaya</s> (deposit of karma).
Because:
This kind of karma is indeed four-footed, that is, fourfold.
It is black, white-and-black, white, and neither white nor black.
Among these, black belongs to evil-minded people.
White-and-black is accomplished by external means; there the accumulation of the <s>karmāśaya</s> occurs precisely through the channels of harming and helping others.
White belongs to those who practice austerity, recitation, and meditation.

children.text: sā hi kevale manasy āyatatvād bahiḥsādhanānadhīnā parān pīḍayitvā bhavati ||
children.translated_text: For because it depends solely on the mind and does not depend on external means, it comes about without harming others.
Neither-white-nor-black belongs to renouncers whose afflictions have been exhausted and who are in their final body.

children.text: tatrāśuklaṃ yogina eva phalasaṃnyāsāt akṛṣṇaṃ cānupādānāt ||
children.translated_text: There it is not white only in the yogin, because he renounces the fruit, and it is not black because he does not take anything up.

children.text: itareṣāṃ tu bhūtānāṃ pūrvam eva trividham iti ||
children.translated_text: But for other beings, the former threefold karma alone exists.
'From that' means from the threefold karma.
Only those that correspond to its fruition are meant.

children.text: yajjātīyasya karmaṇo yo vipākas tasyānuguṇā yā vāsanāḥ karmavipākam anuśerate tāsām evābhivyaktiḥ ||
children.translated_text: The <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions) that correspond to the fruition of a given kind of karma, and that lie dormant alongside the fruition of karma, are the very ones that become manifest.

children.text: na hi daivaṃ karma vipacyamānaṃ nārakatiryaṅmanuṣyavāsanābhivyaktinimittaṃ sambhavati ||
children.translated_text: For divine karma, when it ripens, cannot be the cause for the manifestation of latent impressions belonging to hell-beings, animals, or humans.
Rather, only the latent impressions corresponding to the divine state become manifest in it.
And in hell-beings, animals, and humans the same discussion applies in just this way.
The arising of the fruition of a scorpion's sting is made manifest by the eye-salve that reveals its own object.

children.text: sa yadi jātiśatena vā dūradeśatayā vā kalpaśatena vā vyavahitaḥ punaśca svavyañjakāñjana evodiyād drāg ity evaṃ pūrvānubhūtavṛṣadaṃśavipākābhisaṃskṛtā vāsanā upādāya vyajyeta ||
children.translated_text: If that were separated by a hundred births, by remoteness of place, or by a hundred aeons, and then arose again only when its own revealing eye-salve was present, at once the latent impression conditioned by the previously experienced fruition of a scorpion's sting would become manifest by taking hold of it.
Why?

children.text: yato vyavahitānām apyāsāṃ sadṛśaṃ karmābhivyañjakaṃ nimittībhūtam ity ānantaryam eva ||
children.translated_text: Because, even when they are separated, a similar karma has become the instrumental cause that manifests them; therefore there is direct continuity itself.
And for what further reason?
Because memory and saṃskāra have one form.
As the experiences are, so are the <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions).

children.text: te ca karmavāsanānurūpāḥ yathā ca vāsanās tathā smṛtir iti jātideśakālavyavahitebhyaḥ saṃskārebhyaḥ smṛtiḥ smṛteśca punaḥ saṃskārāḥ ity evam ete smṛtisaṃskārāḥ karmāśayavṛttilābhavaśād vyajyante ||
children.translated_text: And they conform to the karmic latent impressions; and as the latent impressions are, so is memory. Thus from <s>saṃskāras</s> separated by birth, place, and time comes memory, and from memory again come <s>saṃskāras</s>. In this way these memories and <s>saṃskāras</s> become manifest through obtaining the activity of the <s>karmāśaya</s>.

children.text: ataśca vyavahitānām api nimittanaimittikabhāvānucchedād ānantaryam eva siddham iti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, even when they are separated, because the relation of cause and effect is not cut off, direct continuity itself is established.
Because the wish of those latent impressions is eternal, they are beginningless.
This self-wish: why is it so?

children.text: jātamātrasya jantor ananubhūtamaraṇadharmakasya dveṣaduḥkhānusmṛtinimitto maraṇatrāsaḥ kathaṃ bhavet ||
children.translated_text: How could fear of death arise in a creature just born, one that has not experienced the condition of death, unless it had as its cause the recollection of aversion and pain?

children.text: na ca svābhāvikaṃ vastu nimittam upādatte ||
children.translated_text: And a thing that is natural does not take up an external cause.

children.text: tasmād anādivāsanānuviddham idaṃ cittaṃ nimittavaśāt kāścid eva vāsanāḥ pratilabhya puruṣasya bhogāyopāvartata iti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore this mind, pierced through by beginningless latent impressions, recovers only certain latent impressions under the force of a cause and turns toward the experience of <s>puruṣa</s>.

children.text: ghaṭaprāsādapradīpakalpaṃ saṃkocavikāsi cittaṃ śarīraparimāṇākāramātram ity apare pratipannāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Others have accepted that the mind, like a pot, palace, or lamp, contracts and expands, and has only a form the size of the body.
And in that way, they say, an intermediate state and transmigration are reasonable.
But the teacher says that only the activity of this all-pervading mind contracts and expands.
And that depends upon causes such as <s>dharma</s>.

children.text: nimittaṃ ca dvividhaṃ bāhyam ādhyātmikaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: The cause is twofold: external and internal.
The external cause depends on instruments such as the body: praise, giving, respectful salutation, and so forth.
The internal cause, such as faith, depends only on the mind.
And so it is said:

children.text: ye caite maitryādayo dhyāyināṃ vihārās te bāhyasādhananiranugrahātmānaḥ prakṛṣṭaṃ dharmam abhinirvartayanti ||
children.translated_text: These modes of dwelling for meditators, beginning with friendliness, whose nature is unaided by external means, produce excellent <s>dharma</s>.
Of the two, the mental one is stronger.
How so?
By what can knowledge and dispassion be surpassed?

children.text: daṇḍakāraṇyaṃ ca cittabalavyatirekeṇa kaḥ śārīreṇa karmaṇā śūnyaṃ kartum utsaheta ||
children.translated_text: And who, apart from the power of mind, could undertake to make the <s>Daṇḍakāraṇya</s> empty by bodily action?
Or drink the ocean like <s>Agastya</s>?

children.text: hetur dharmāt sukham adharmād duḥkhaṃ sukhād rāgo duḥkhād dveṣas tataśca prayatnas tena manasā vācā kāyena vā parispandamānaḥ param anugṛhṇāty upahanti vā ||
children.translated_text: The cause is this: from <s>dharma</s> comes pleasure; from <s>adharma</s>, pain; from pleasure, attachment; from pain, aversion; and from that, effort. By that effort, moving through mind, speech, or body, one either benefits another or harms another.

children.text: tataḥ punar dharmādharmau sukhaduḥkhe rāgadveṣāv iti pravṛttim idaṃ ṣaḍaraṃ saṃsāracakram ||
children.translated_text: From that again come <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, pleasure and pain, attachment and aversion. This activity is the six-spoked wheel of <s>saṃsāra</s>.

children.text: asya ca pratikṣaṇam āvartamānasyāvidyā netrī mūlaṃ sarvakleśānām ity eṣa hetuḥ ||
children.translated_text: As this turns at every moment, ignorance is its guide and the root of all the afflictions: this is the cause.

children.text: phalaṃ tu yam āśritya yasya pratyutpannatā dharmādeḥ na hy apūrvopajanaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But the fruit is that on which the present manifestation of <s>dharma</s> and the rest depends; for there is no production of something unprecedented.
The mind, so long as it has its function, is the support of the latent impressions.

children.text: na hy avasitādhikāre manasi nirāśrayā vāsanāḥ sthātum utsahante ||
children.translated_text: For when the mind's function has ceased, unsupported latent impressions cannot remain.

children.text: yad abhimukhībhūtaṃ vastu yāṃ vāsanāṃ vyanakti tasyās tad ālambanam ||
children.translated_text: The object that has come into focus and manifests a particular latent impression is the support-object of that impression.

children.text: evaṃ hetuphalāśrayālambanair etaiḥ saṃgṛhītāḥ sarvā vāsanāḥ ||
children.translated_text: In this way all latent impressions are included under these: cause, fruit, support, and object.

children.text: eṣām abhāve tatsaṃśrayāṇām api vāsanānām abhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When these are absent, the latent impressions that depend on them are also absent.

children.text: nāsty asataḥ saṃbhavaḥ na cāsti sato vināśa iti dravyatvena sambhavantyaḥ kathaṃ nivartiṣyante vāsanā iti ||
children.translated_text: But, it may be asked, since what is nonexistent cannot arise, and what exists cannot be destroyed, how will latent impressions, which exist as real substances, cease?

children.text: bhaviṣyadvyaktikam anāgatam anubhūtavyaktikam atītam svavyāpāroparūḍhaṃ vartamānam ||
children.translated_text: The future is that whose manifestation is yet to come; the past is that whose manifestation has been experienced; the present is that which has entered upon its own activity.
And these three are the object, the knowable, of knowledge.

children.text: yadi caitat svarūpato nābhaviṣyan nedaṃ nirviṣayaṃ jñānam udapatsyata tasmād atītānāgataṃ svarūpato 'stīti ||
children.translated_text: For if this did not exist in its own nature, this knowledge would arise without an object. Therefore the past and the future exist in their own nature.

children.text: kiṃca bhogabhāgīyasya vāpavargabhāgīyasya vā karmaṇaḥ phalam utpitsu yadi nirupākhyam iti tad uddeśena tena nimittena kuśalānuṣṭhānaṃ na yujyate ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, when the fruit of an action leading either to experience or to liberation is about to arise, if that fruit were indescribable as nonexistent, then the performance of wholesome acts with that as their aim and occasion would not be intelligible.

children.text: sataśca phalasya nimittaṃ vartamānīkaraṇe samarthaṃ nāpūrvopajanane ||
children.translated_text: And the occasion is capable of making an already existent fruit present, not of producing something unprecedented.

children.text: siddhaṃ nimittaṃ naimittikasya viśeṣānugrahaṃ kurute nāpūrvam utpādayatīti ||
children.translated_text: An established occasion gives a special assistance to what depends on it; it does not produce something unprecedented.
And the bearer of properties has a nature consisting of many properties.
Its properties are arranged according to the distinction of temporal paths.

children.text: na ca yathā vartamānaṃ vyaktiviśeṣāpannaṃ dravyato 'sty evam atītam anāgataṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Yet the past and future do not exist substantially in the same way as the present, which has assumed a particular manifestation.
How then?

children.text: svenaiva vyaṅgyena svarūpeṇānāgatam asti svena cānubhūtavyaktikena svarūpeṇātītam iti vartamānasyaivādhvanaḥ svarūpavyaktir iti na sā bhavaty atītānāgatayor adhvanoḥ ||
children.translated_text: The future exists in its own form as that which is to be manifested, and the past in its own form as that whose manifestation has been experienced. Thus the manifestation of its own form belongs only to the present temporal path; it does not belong to the past and future temporal paths.

children.text: ekasya cādhvanaḥ samaye dvāv adhvānau dharmisamanvāgatau bhavata eveti nābhūtvā bhāvas trayāṇām adhvanām iti ||
children.translated_text: And at the time of one temporal path, the two other temporal paths are indeed connected with the bearer of properties; therefore the three temporal paths do not come into being after having been nonexistent.

children.text: te khalv amī tryadhvāno dharmā vartamānā vyaktātmāno 'tītānāgatāḥ sūkṣmātmānaḥ sarvam idaṃ guṇānāṃ saṃniveśaviśeṣamātram iti paramārthato guṇātmānaḥ
children.translated_text: These properties, then, in the three temporal paths, are manifest in their present form and subtle in their past and future forms. All this is nothing but a particular arrangement of the <s>guṇas</s>; ultimately its nature is the <s>guṇas</s>.
And so there is the instruction of scripture:

children.text: guṇānāṃ paramaṃ rūpaṃ na dṛṣṭipatham ṛcchati
children.translated_text: The supreme form of the <s>guṇas</s> does not come within the range of sight;

children.text: yat tu dṛṣṭipathaṃ prāptaṃ tan māyeva sutucchakam ||
children.translated_text: but what has come within the range of sight is very slight, like an illusion.
Thus.

children.text: yadā tu sarve guṇāḥ katham ekaḥ śabda ekam indriyam iti ||
children.translated_text: But if all are <s>guṇas</s>, how is there one sound and one sense-faculty?

children.text: prakhyākriyāsthitiśīlānāṃ guṇānāṃ grahaṇātmakānāṃ karaṇabhāvenaikaḥ pariṇāmaḥ śrotram indriyam
children.translated_text: Because of the <s>guṇas</s>, whose nature is illumination, activity, and stability, one transformation as an instrument, consisting in grasping, is the auditory sense-faculty.

children.text: grāhyātmakānāṃ śabdatanmātrabhāvenaikaḥ pariṇāmaḥ śabdo viṣaya iti
children.translated_text: One transformation of those same <s>guṇas</s> as the subtle element of sound, consisting in what is grasped, is sound as an object.

children.text: śabdādīnāṃ mūrtisamānajātīyānām ekaḥ pariṇāmaḥ pṛthivīparamāṇus tanmātrāvayavaḥ
children.translated_text: One transformation of sound and the other subtle elements, belonging to the same class as embodied form, is the earth-atom, a constituent part of the subtle elements.

children.text: teṣāṃ caikaḥ pariṇāmaḥ pṛthivī gaur vṛkṣaḥ parvata ity evamādi
children.translated_text: And one transformation of these is earth, a cow, a tree, a mountain, and so on.

children.text: bhūtāntareṣv api snehauṣṇyapraṇāmitvāvakāśadānāny upādāya sāmānyam ekavikārārambhaḥ samādheyaḥ
children.translated_text: In the case of the other elements too, taking into account cohesion, heat, yielding motion, and the giving of space, one should understand the general principle that a single modification is begun.

children.text: nāsty artho vijñānavisahacaraḥ asti tu jñānam arthavisahacaraṃ svapnādau kalpitam ity anayā diśā ye vastusvarūpam apahnuvate jñānaparikalpanāmātraṃ vastu svapnaviṣayopamaṃ kutaścaitad anyāyyam ||
children.translated_text: There is no object separated from cognition; but there is cognition separated from an object, imagined in dreams and the like. Those who, by this line of reasoning, deny the real nature of objects and claim that an object is merely a construction of knowledge, like the object of a dream: why is this unjustified?
A single object, being the support of many minds, is common.

children.text: tat khalu naikacittaparikalpitaṃ nāpy anekacittaparikalpitaṃ kiṃtu svapratiṣṭham
children.translated_text: It is not constructed by one mind, nor constructed by many minds; rather, it is established in itself.
How so?
Because, while the object is the same, minds differ.

children.text: dharmāpekṣaṃ cittasya vastusāmye 'pi sukhajñānaṃ bhavaty adharmāpekṣaṃ tata eva duḥkhajñānam avidyāpekṣaṃ tata eva mūḍhajñānaṃ samyagdarśanāpekṣaṃ tata eva mādhyasthyajñānam iti
children.translated_text: Even when the object is the same, depending on <s>dharma</s> the mind has a cognition of pleasure from it; depending on <s>adharma</s>, from that very same thing, a cognition of pain; depending on ignorance, from that very same thing, a confused cognition; depending on right vision, from that very same thing, a cognition of neutrality.
By whose mind, then, has that object been constructed?
Nor is it reasonable that the mind of one person should be colored by an object constructed by another mind.
Therefore the paths of object and knowledge, divided by the difference between what is grasped and what grasps, are distinct.
There is not even the slightest trace of confusion between the two.

children.text: sāṃkhyapakṣe punar vastu triguṇaṃ calaṃ ca guṇavṛttam iti dharmādinimittāpekṣaṃ cittair abhisaṃbadhyate nimittānurūpasya ca pratyayasyotpadyamānasya tena tenātmanā hetur bhavati ||
children.translated_text: On the Sāṃkhya view, moreover, the object is composed of the three <s>guṇas</s>, is changeable, and is an activity of the <s>guṇas</s>; depending on occasions such as <s>dharma</s>, it becomes connected with minds, and, for a cognition arising in accordance with the occasion, it becomes the cause in each corresponding form.
Some say:
The object arises together with knowledge, because it is something to be experienced, like pleasure and the rest.

children.text: ta etayā dvārā sādhāraṇatvaṃ bādhamānāḥ pūrvottarakṣaṇeṣu vasturūpam evāpahnuvate ||
children.translated_text: They, in refuting commonality through this approach, deny the very form of the object in the preceding and following moments.

children.text: ekacittatantraṃ ced vastu syāt tadā citte vyagre niruddhe vāsvarūpam eva tenāparāmṛṣṭam anyasyāviṣayībhūtam apramāṇakam agṛhītam asvabhāvakaṃ kenacit tadānīṃ kiṃ tat syāt
children.translated_text: If an object were dependent on one mind, then, when that mind is distracted or restrained, what would that object be at that time, untouched by that mind, not made an object for another, without a means of knowledge, ungrasped, and devoid of its own nature?
And when it was again connected with the mind, from where would it arise?

children.text: ye cāsyānupasthitā bhāgās te cāsya na syur evaṃ nāsti pṛṣṭham ity udaram api na gṛhyeta
children.translated_text: And the parts of it that are not present to that mind would not exist. In that case, since the back is not seen, the belly too would not be grasped.

children.text: tasmāt svatantro 'rthaḥ sarvapuruṣasādhāraṇaḥ svatantrāṇi ca cittāni pratipuruṣaṃ pravartante
children.translated_text: Therefore the object is independent and common to all <s>puruṣas</s>, and independent minds operate for each individual <s>puruṣa</s>.

children.text: tayoḥ saṃbandhād upalabdhiḥ puruṣasya bhoga iti ||
children.translated_text: From the conjunction of the two arises apprehension; this is the experience of <s>puruṣa</s>.

children.text: ayaskāntamaṇikalpā viṣayā ayaḥsadharmakaṃ cittam abhisaṃbadhyoparañjayanti yena ca viṣayeṇoparaktaṃ cittaṃ sa viṣayo jñātas tato 'nyaḥ punar ajñātaḥ
children.translated_text: Objects, like lodestones, bring the mind, which has a nature like iron, into connection with themselves and color it; and the object by which the mind is colored is known, while another is unknown.
Because a thing has the nature of being known and unknown, the mind is subject to transformation.

children.text: yasya tu tad eva cittaṃ viṣayas tasya ||
children.translated_text: But for one for whom that very mind is the object,

children.text: yadi cittavat prabhur api puruṣaḥ pariṇameta tatas tadviṣayāścittavṛttayaḥ śabdādiviṣayavaj jñātāḥ syuḥ
children.translated_text: if <s>puruṣa</s>, the master, were to transform just as the mind does, then mental modifications whose object is that would be known, like modifications whose objects are sound and the rest.

children.text: sadājñātatvaṃ tu manasas tatprabhoḥ puruṣasyāpariṇāmitvam anumāpayati ||
children.translated_text: But the fact that the mind is always known leads one to infer the non-transformability of <s>puruṣa</s>, its master.

children.text: syād āśaṅkā cittam eva svābhāsaṃ viṣayābhāsaṃ ca bhaviṣyaty agnivat ||
children.translated_text: There may be the objection: the mind itself will be both self-illuminating and object-illuminating, like fire.

children.text: yathetarāṇīndriyāṇi śabdādayaśca dṛśyatvān na svābhāsāni tathā mano 'pi pratyetavyam
children.translated_text: Just as the other senses and sound and the rest, because they are seen, are not self-illuminating, so too the mind should be understood.
Nor is fire an example here.

children.text: na hy agnir ātmasvarūpam aprakāśaṃ prakāśayati
children.translated_text: For fire does not illuminate its own nature as something previously unilluminated.
And this illumination is observed where illuminator and illuminated are conjoined.
But in mere self-nature there is no conjunction.

children.text: kiṃca svābhāsaṃ cittam ity agrāhyam eva kasyacid iti śabdārthaḥ
children.translated_text: Moreover, the statement that the mind is self-illuminating means precisely that it is not graspable by anyone.
For example:

children.text: svātmapratiṣṭham ākāśaṃ na parapratiṣṭham ity arthaḥ
children.translated_text: the meaning of 'space rests on itself, not on another' is just this.
The activity of living beings is seen from their awareness of the movement of their own intellect.

children.text: kruddho 'haṃ bhīto 'ham amutra me rāgo 'mutra me krodha iti
children.translated_text: 'I am angry,' 'I am afraid,' 'I have attachment there,' 'I have anger there' - thus they speak.

children.text: etat svabuddher agrahaṇe na yuktam iti ||
children.translated_text: This would not be reasonable if one's own intellect were not grasped.
Nor is determination of one's own nature reasonable in a single moment.

children.text: kṣaṇikavādino yad bhavanaṃ saiva kriyā tad eva ca kārakam ity abhyupagamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For the momentarists accept that the very becoming of a thing is its action, and that same thing is the agent.

children.text: syān matiḥ svarasaniruddhaṃ cittaṃ cittāntareṇa samanantareṇa gṛhyata iti ||
children.translated_text: There may be the thought: a mind that has ceased in its own flavor is grasped by another immediately subsequent mind.

children.text: atha cittaṃ cec cittāntareṇa gṛhyeta buddhibuddhiḥ kena gṛhyate sāpy anyayā sāpy anyayeti atiprasaṅgaḥ smṛtisaṃkaraśca yāvanto buddhibuddhīnām anubhavās tāvatyaḥ smṛtayaḥ prāpnuvanti
children.translated_text: But if a mind were grasped by another mind, by what is the cognition of that cognition grasped? By another, and that too by another: thus there is excessive regress, and also confusion of memory; as many experiences of cognitions of cognitions as there are, so many memories would follow.
And because of their confusion, there would be no ascertainment of a single memory.

children.text: evaṃ buddhipratisaṃvedinaṃ puruṣam apalapadbhir vaināśikaiḥ sarvam evākulīkṛtam
children.translated_text: Thus, by the <s>Vaināśikas</s>, who deny <s>puruṣa</s> as the one who is aware of cognition, everything has been thrown into disorder.

children.text: te tu bhoktṛsvarūpaṃ yatra kvacana kalpayanto na nyāyena saṃgacchante
children.translated_text: And when they imagine the nature of an experiencer somewhere or other, they do not fit with reason.

children.text: kecit tu sattvamātram api parikalpyāsti sa sattvo ya etān pañca skandhān nikṣipyānyāṃśca pratisaṃdadhātīty uktvā tata eva punas trasyanti
children.translated_text: Some, moreover, after positing even a mere sentient being, saying, 'There is that sentient being who casts off these five <s>skandhas</s> and links up others,' then become afraid of that very position.

children.text: tathā skandhānāṃ mahānirvedāya virāgāyānutpādāya praśāntaye guror antike brahmacaryaṃ cariṣyāmi ity uktvā sattvasya punaḥ sattvam evāpahnuvate
children.translated_text: Likewise, after saying, 'For the great disenchantment with the <s>skandhas</s>, for dispassion, for non-arising, for tranquillity, I will practice celibate discipline in the presence of a teacher,' they again deny the sentient being its very sentience.

children.text: sāṃkhyayogādayas tu pravādāḥ svaśabdena puruṣam eva svāminaṃ cittasya bhoktāram upayantīti ||
children.translated_text: But doctrines such as <s>Sāṃkhya</s> and <s>Yoga</s>, by their own terminology, accept <s>puruṣa</s> alone as the master of the mind and the experiencer.
How?
When knowledge is freed from all coverings of affliction and karma, it becomes infinite.

children.text: āvarakeṇa tamasābhibhūtam āvṛtam anantaṃ jñānasattvaṃ kvacid eva rajasā pravartitam udghāṭitaṃ grahaṇasamarthaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: The infinite knowledge-<s>sattva</s>, overpowered and covered by the concealing darkness, when set in motion somewhere by <s>rajas</s>, becomes opened up and capable of apprehension.

children.text: tatra yadā sarvair āvaraṇamalair apagataṃ bhavati tadā bhavaty asyānantyam ||
children.translated_text: There, when it has been rid of all covering impurities, then its infinitude comes about.

children.text: jñānasyānantyājjñeyam alpaṃ sampadyate yathā yatredam uktam
children.translated_text: Because knowledge is infinite, the knowable becomes small, as in the place where this is said:

children.text: andho maṇim avidhyat tam anaṅgulir āvayat
children.translated_text: The blind man pierced the jewel; the fingerless man strung it.
The neckless man put it on, and the tongueless man praised it.
Thus.
